items.title: What Claude actually gets from a screen recording, token counts for 4 ways to send it
items.summary: Claude can't open your screen recording. Anthropic's vision docs list JPEG, PNG, GIF and WebP as input formats, and for a GIF only the first frame is used. Codex and ChatGPT take images too, not MP4. So when a bug needs a 43 second repro, something has to turn the video into what the model can read. I tried four ways on the same recording: 43 seconds, 3 screens, a few clicks on X.com. 1. Still frames Each frame is an image, and Claude 4.7 counts image tokens in 28px patches: ceil(width/28) x ceil(height/28). A 1440x900 frame is 52 x 33 = 1,716 tokens. One frame per screen is 3 frames, about 5,150 tokens. One frame per second is 43 frames, about 73,800 tokens, and once a request carries more than 20 images the per-image size limit gets stricter. Either way the clicks are gone. You see the screen before and after, not which button was pressed. 2. One tall stitched page Stitching the whole flow into one long image looks clever and costs almost nothing. That's the problem. Claude 4.7 shrinks any image to 2576px on the long edge (older models 1568px). A 2540x18410 page arrives as 355x2576, about 1,196 tokens, and 16px body text ends up around 2.2px tall. On older models it's 216x1568 and 1.4px. The same thing happens with Playwright fullPage: true captures. Odilon Hugonnot's CLAUDE.md for mobile redesign uses full-page screenshot scripts at 375 to 768px, and on a long mobile page those get squeezed the same way before Claude checks them. Crop to the viewport, or slice the page into tiles with a small overlap so a line cut at the seam still shows whole in one tile. 3. Gemini, which does take video Gemini is the one model here that accepts video. It samples 1 frame per second at about 100 tokens per second at default resolution, so the 43 second clip is about 4,300 tokens. Cheapest of the four. It still only sees one frame a second, so a quick click between two samples can disappear, and you're outside Claude or Codex for that question. 4. The recording as JSON This one skips pixels. SlimSnap records the screen with voice and writes JSON next to the MP4: one frame per screen with its text and positions, every click with the control it hit and the screen it led to, and each spoken sentence tied to the element under the pointer. The same 43 seconds came to 6.3k tokens of JSON. It costs more than Gemini and far less than a frame per second. What you get for it is that "I clicked Save and nothing happened" reaches the model as the actual control plus the screen that came after. Which one to send You want to show Send One screen One cropped screenshot A long page Viewport-sized tiles, not one tall image A flow, and you use Gemini The MP4 A flow, and you use Claude or Codex One frame per screen, or JSON with the clicks Reproduce the numbers Tokens for one image on Claude 4.7: python3 -c "import math;w,h=1440,900;print(math.ceil(w/28)*math.ceil(h/28))" The size Claude actually sees for a tall page: python3 -c "w,h=2540,18410;s=2576/max(w,h);print(round(w*s),round(h*s))" A still at each screen change, to send as frames: ffmpeg -ss 4.5 -i repro.mp4 -frames:v 1 screen2.png
items.summary_html:
Claude can't open your screen recording. Anthropic's vision docs list JPEG, PNG, GIF and WebP as input formats, and for a GIF only the first frame is used. Codex and ChatGPT take images too, not MP4.

So when a bug needs a 43 second repro, something has to turn the video into what the model can read. I tried four ways on the same recording: 43 seconds, 3 screens, a few clicks on X.com.

1. Still frames

Each frame is an image, and Claude 4.7 counts image tokens in 28px patches: ceil(width/28) x ceil(height/28). A 1440x900 frame is 52 x 33 = 1,716 tokens.

One frame per screen is 3 frames, about 5,150 tokens. One frame per second is 43 frames, about 73,800 tokens, and once a request carries more than 20 images the per-image size limit gets stricter.

Either way the clicks are gone. You see the screen before and after, not which button was pressed.

2. One tall stitched page

Stitching the whole flow into one long image looks clever and costs almost nothing. That's the problem.

Claude 4.7 shrinks any image to 2576px on the long edge (older models 1568px). A 2540x18410 page arrives as 355x2576, about 1,196 tokens, and 16px body text ends up around 2.2px tall. On older models it's 216x1568 and 1.4px.

The same thing happens with Playwright fullPage: true captures. Odilon Hugonnot's CLAUDE.md for mobile redesign uses full-page screenshot scripts at 375 to 768px, and on a long mobile page those get squeezed the same way before Claude checks them. Crop to the viewport, or slice the page into tiles with a small overlap so a line cut at the seam still shows whole in one tile.

3. Gemini, which does take video

Gemini is the one model here that accepts video. It samples 1 frame per second at about 100 tokens per second at default resolution, so the 43 second clip is about 4,300 tokens.

Cheapest of the four. It still only sees one frame a second, so a quick click between two samples can disappear, and you're outside Claude or Codex for that question.

4. The recording as JSON

This one skips pixels. SlimSnap records the screen with voice and writes JSON next to the MP4: one frame per screen with its text and positions, every click with the control it hit and the screen it led to, and each spoken sentence tied to the element under the pointer.

The same 43 seconds came to 6.3k tokens of JSON.

It costs more than Gemini and far less than a frame per second. What you get for it is that "I clicked Save and nothing happened" reaches the model as the actual control plus the screen that came after.

Which one to send
You want to show Send One screen One cropped screenshot A long page Viewport-sized tiles, not one tall image A flow, and you use Gemini The MP4 A flow, and you use Claude or Codex One frame per screen, or JSON with the clicks
Reproduce the numbers

Tokens for one image on Claude 4.7:

python3 -c "import math;w,h=1440,900;print(math.ceil(w/28)*math.ceil(h/28))"

The size Claude actually sees for a tall page:

python3 -c "w,h=2540,18410;s=2576/max(w,h);print(round(w*s),round(h*s))"

A still at each screen change, to send as frames:

ffmpeg -ss 4.5 -i repro.mp4 -frames:v 1 screen2.png

items.title: CoreWeave’s CEO isn’t panicking about Nvidia losing Jensen Huang
items.summary: CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator called Huang a visionary, but said the rest of the AI supply chain will continue to be supported by Nvidia, even in Huang's absence. Bloomberg/Getty Images If CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator is worried about Jensen Huang's exit from Nvidia, he isn't showing it. Intrator said that CoreWeave and Nvidia's partnership would continue even in Huang's absence. Nvidia is a major backer and supplier of neocloud companies like CoreWeave. A major neocloud executive doesn't seem phased by Jensen Huang's departure from Nvidia. CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator, at Semafor's "Silicon Valley & The World" event on Tuesday, hinted that he wasn't overly concerned about how Huang's departure from Nvidia would affect CoreWeave's business. He said that Nvidia has been an "extraordinary company," but it also employs "thousands and thousands of amazing engineers and employees" who would continue their partnership. "Those thousands of people integrate with CoreWeave every day to work on how you deploy the equipment, how you build the data centers, how you network the infrastructure, all of these things, and you know, that continues," Intrator added. The moderator asked if Huang's absence — even if just emotionally — would be felt when it came to accessing credit for data center infrastructure. Huang was a huge backer of neocloud companies like CoreWeave. Intrator said that Huang was a visionary who supported not just Nvidia but the data center and AI ecosystem . But the reason Huang propped the ecosystem up was because these elements of the supply chain "were needed and they will continue to be needed, and they will continue to be supported by Nvidia and by the balance sheet that they represent," he said. Intrator's comments came after a tumultuous week for Nvidia, where Huang resigned after multiple allegations emerged over his extramarital affairs. But the pessimism didn't extend to Nvidia's earnings call on Tuesday, where the chipmaker reported revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year earlier. Nvidia's stock price was up more than 4% in after-hours trading, and Nvidia's leadership said it wasn't considering bringing Huang back. Neoclouds — cloud computing services specifically for AI customers — made headlines in October for their high debt levels to build AI capacity, but the returns on that investment remain unclear. Investors were spooked by the uncertainty, and their stocks took a major hit. Huang, while he was still with Nvidia, maintained that demand for AI cloud infrastructure is "off the charts." Nvidia is a major supplier to and backer of neocloud companies such as CoreWeave, Nebius, and Iren. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: One semantic model, four tools: the same numbers and the same permissions
items.summary: Applies to eMondrian Community release 2026.11.16.1 and later. Different people may see different parts of the same data. A regional manager may see their region only; finance may see costs and margins, sales may not. Without access rules in the model, there are two options: a separate copy of the report or model for each audience, or everyone sees everything. Row-level and object-level security give a third option: one model and one report, and each user sees only what they are allowed to see. In eMondrian the rules live in one place: the semantic model. Excel, Power BI, eMondrian Dashboard and AI agents over MCP all query the same model, and the model decides what each user sees. Row-level and object-level security A semantic model answers two questions about every user: which data may they see, and which parts of the model may they see. Row-level security (RLS) limits the data. Two users open the same report and see different rows: a regional manager sees their region, a store manager sees their store. The report, the measures and the dimensions are the same for both; the rows and the totals are different. Object-level security (OLS) limits the model itself. A measure, a hierarchy or a whole dimension can be hidden from a user. For that user the object doesn't exist: it isn't in the field list, and a query that names it gets an error. Typical cases are costs and margins, salaries, or customer details. In eMondrian both are set with roles in the schema. A role lists what its users may see: cubes, dimensions, hierarchies, members and measures. Users get roles through their groups. The server applies the role to every query, whichever tool sent it. The model The example uses the FoodMart sample, cube Sales , year 1997. Three states have sales: Store State Unit Sales CA 74,748 OR 67,659 WA 124,366 Total 266,773 The schema has two roles and a default role: Sales-A sees California only. Sales-B sees Washington only. Store Cost, the Weekly hierarchy of Time and the Promotions dimension are hidden from it. No Access is the default role: a user with neither role sees no cubes. name = "No Access" > access = "none" /> name = "Sales-A" > access = "none" > cube = "Sales" access = "all" > hierarchy = "[Store]" access = "custom" rollupPolicy = "partial" > member = "[Store].[USA].[CA]" access = "all" /> name = "/Sales-A" /> name = "Sales-B" > access = "none" > cube = "Sales" access = "all" > hierarchy = "[Store]" access = "custom" rollupPolicy = "partial" > member = "[Store].[USA].[WA]" access = "all" /> hierarchy = "[Measures]" access = "custom" > member = "[Measures].[Store Cost]" access = "none" /> hierarchy = "[Time.Weekly]" access = "none" /> dimension = "[Promotions]" access = "none" /> name = "/Sales-B" /> RoleMember names a group by its full path. With authentication on, eMondrian takes the user's groups at every request and applies the matching roles. The schema sets defaultRole="No Access" . Three users: User Group Role user-a /Sales-A Sales-A user-b /Sales-B Sales-B user-c — No Access Four tools, three users Each user asked the same question in each tool: Unit Sales by Store State, 1997. Tool user-a user-b user-c Excel (PivotTable) CA 74,748 WA 124,366 Cube not found Power BI (live connection) CA 74,748 WA 124,366 Cube not found eMondrian Dashboard CA 74,748 WA 124,366 Dashboard not found AI agent over MCP CA 74,748 WA 124,366 No cubes The numbers match in every tool, because every tool asks the same model. Excel sends MDX, Power BI sends DAX, the dashboard and the agent send queries through the same server. The role is applied inside the server, before any query reaches the database. The dashboard was built by the administrator and shared with the groups /Sales-A and /Sales-B with Can view . Each viewer sees the same dashboard with their own data: the visuals read their data with the viewer's roles. user-c has no right on the dashboard, so it opens as not found. See Dashboard access . Rows: each user sees their own states The role lists the members a user may see. Everything else is filtered out in every query: on rows, in filters and in totals. The totals depend on rollupPolicy : rollupPolicy Total for user-a partial 74,748, the sum of the visible states full 266,773, the total of all states With full , the total row shows the company's full figure to a user who sees one state. For row-level security, use partial : the total is the sum of what the user may see, in all four tools. Objects: measures, hierarchies and dimensions Object-level security hides parts of the model itself. For user-b, three objects are hidden. A measure. Store Cost isn't in the field list of Excel or Power BI, isn't returned by the agent's describe_cube , and isn't offered in the dashboard. A query that names it gets an error, in MDX and in DAX: MDX object '[Measures].[Store Cost]' not found Calculated measures built on a hidden measure are hidden too. Profit is Store Sales minus Store Cost, so user-b doesn't see Profit or Profit Growth either. The margin can't be worked out from what remains. A hierarchy. The Time dimension has two hierarchies: Time (Year, Quarter, Month) and Weekly (Year, Week, Day). user-b sees Time; Weekly is hidden. It isn't in the field list, in describe_cube or in the dashboard, and a query that names it gets an error. A dimension. The whole Promotions dimension, with all its hierarchies, is hidden from user-b. For the user, a hidden object doesn't exist: there is nothing to click and nothing to ask about. The agent acts as the user An AI agent connected over MCP signs in as a user and gets that user's roles. When user-b asks the agent for store costs, the agent's tools don't know the measure: the model it sees has no Store Cost. Every MCP call is written to logs/mcp-audit.log with the name of the user. Summary One model, one set of rules: roles in the schema. Excel, Power BI, eMondrian Dashboard and AI agents get the same numbers for the same user. Rows: members per role, with rollupPolicy="partial" for honest totals. Objects: measures, calculated measures built on them, hierarchies and dimensions. Groups come from Keycloak, Active Directory or LDAP; see Security and Roles in the schema . eMondrian: Demo · GitHub · Docs More: Security · Roles in the schema · Dashboard access
items.summary_html:
Applies to eMondrian Community release 2026.11.16.1 and later.

Different people may see different parts of the same data. A regional manager may see their region only; finance may see costs and margins, sales may not. Without access rules in the model, there are two options: a separate copy of the report or model for each audience, or everyone sees everything.

Row-level and object-level security give a third option: one model and one report, and each user sees only what they are allowed to see.

In eMondrian the rules live in one place: the semantic model. Excel, Power BI, eMondrian Dashboard and AI agents over MCP all query the same model, and the model decides what each user sees.

Row-level and object-level security

A semantic model answers two questions about every user: which data may they see, and which parts of the model may they see.

Row-level security (RLS) limits the data. Two users open the same report and see different rows: a regional manager sees their region, a store manager sees their store. The report, the measures and the dimensions are the same for both; the rows and the totals are different.

Object-level security (OLS) limits the model itself. A measure, a hierarchy or a whole dimension can be hidden from a user. For that user the object doesn't exist: it isn't in the field list, and a query that names it gets an error. Typical cases are costs and margins, salaries, or customer details.

In eMondrian both are set with roles in the schema. A role lists what its users may see: cubes, dimensions, hierarchies, members and measures. Users get roles through their groups. The server applies the role to every query, whichever tool sent it.

The model

The example uses the FoodMart sample, cube Sales, year 1997. Three states have sales:

Store State Unit Sales CA 74,748 OR 67,659 WA 124,366 Total 266,773

The schema has two roles and a default role:

  • Sales-A sees California only.
  • Sales-B sees Washington only. Store Cost, the Weekly hierarchy of Time and the Promotions dimension are hidden from it.
  • No Access is the default role: a user with neither role sees no cubes. 
 name="No Access">
   access="none"/>


 name="Sales-A">
   access="none">
     cube="Sales" access="all">
       hierarchy="[Store]" access="custom" rollupPolicy="partial">
         member="[Store].[USA].[CA]" access="all"/>
      
    
  
   name="/Sales-A"/>


 name="Sales-B">
   access="none">
     cube="Sales" access="all">
       hierarchy="[Store]" access="custom" rollupPolicy="partial">
         member="[Store].[USA].[WA]" access="all"/>
      
       hierarchy="[Measures]" access="custom">
         member="[Measures].[Store Cost]" access="none"/>
      
       hierarchy="[Time.Weekly]" access="none"/>
       dimension="[Promotions]" access="none"/>
    
  
   name="/Sales-B"/>

RoleMember names a group by its full path. With authentication on, eMondrian takes the user's groups at every request and applies the matching roles. The schema sets defaultRole="No Access".

Three users:

User Group Role user-a /Sales-A Sales-A user-b /Sales-B Sales-B user-c — No Access
Four tools, three users

Each user asked the same question in each tool: Unit Sales by Store State, 1997.

Tool user-a user-b user-c Excel (PivotTable) CA 74,748 WA 124,366 Cube not found Power BI (live connection) CA 74,748 WA 124,366 Cube not found eMondrian Dashboard CA 74,748 WA 124,366 Dashboard not found AI agent over MCP CA 74,748 WA 124,366 No cubes

The numbers match in every tool, because every tool asks the same model. Excel sends MDX, Power BI sends DAX, the dashboard and the agent send queries through the same server. The role is applied inside the server, before any query reaches the database.

The dashboard was built by the administrator and shared with the groups /Sales-A and /Sales-B with Can view. Each viewer sees the same dashboard with their own data: the visuals read their data with the viewer's roles. user-c has no right on the dashboard, so it opens as not found. See Dashboard access.

Rows: each user sees their own states

The role lists the members a user may see. Everything else is filtered out in every query: on rows, in filters and in totals.

The totals depend on rollupPolicy:

rollupPolicy Total for user-a partial 74,748, the sum of the visible states full 266,773, the total of all states

With full, the total row shows the company's full figure to a user who sees one state. For row-level security, use partial: the total is the sum of what the user may see, in all four tools.

Objects: measures, hierarchies and dimensions

Object-level security hides parts of the model itself. For user-b, three objects are hidden.

A measure. Store Cost isn't in the field list of Excel or Power BI, isn't returned by the agent's describe_cube, and isn't offered in the dashboard. A query that names it gets an error, in MDX and in DAX:

MDX object '[Measures].[Store Cost]' not found

Calculated measures built on a hidden measure are hidden too. Profit is Store Sales minus Store Cost, so user-b doesn't see Profit or Profit Growth either. The margin can't be worked out from what remains.

A hierarchy. The Time dimension has two hierarchies: Time (Year, Quarter, Month) and Weekly (Year, Week, Day). user-b sees Time; Weekly is hidden. It isn't in the field list, in describe_cube or in the dashboard, and a query that names it gets an error.

A dimension. The whole Promotions dimension, with all its hierarchies, is hidden from user-b.

For the user, a hidden object doesn't exist: there is nothing to click and nothing to ask about.

The agent acts as the user

An AI agent connected over MCP signs in as a user and gets that user's roles. When user-b asks the agent for store costs, the agent's tools don't know the measure: the model it sees has no Store Cost.

Every MCP call is written to logs/mcp-audit.log with the name of the user.

Summary
  • One model, one set of rules: roles in the schema.
  • Excel, Power BI, eMondrian Dashboard and AI agents get the same numbers for the same user.
  • Rows: members per role, with rollupPolicy="partial" for honest totals.
  • Objects: measures, calculated measures built on them, hierarchies and dimensions.
  • Groups come from Keycloak, Active Directory or LDAP; see Security and Roles in the schema.

eMondrian: Demo · GitHub · Docs

items.title: A plain checklist to see if ChatGPT and Google AI can read your website
items.summary: Many business sites look fine to people but are hard for search engines and AI tools to read. Here is a short checklist you can run in about 15 minutes. Can crawlers get in? Open yourdomain.com/robots.txt. Make sure it does not block Googlebot or the AI crawlers you want (GPTBot, PerplexityBot, ClaudeBot). Is there a sitemap? Open yourdomain.com/sitemap.xml. It should list your real pages and nothing broken. Does each page have one clear title and one H1 that say what the page is about? Do your answers appear as plain text near the top of the page? AI tools quote short direct answers, so put the answer first and the detail after. Do you have basic structured data (Organization, and FAQ where it fits)? Test it with Google's Rich Results Test. Is the page fast and readable on a phone? Run PageSpeed Insights. Is your business name, site and contact the same everywhere you are listed? Fix these in order. None of them needs a big budget. They just need someone to check. We are Liftup Technologies, a team of 10 in Pune that has worked on websites, SEO and automation since 2015. We built a free tool that checks the AI side of this: https://liftup.tech/tools/ai-visibility-checker/ What is the first thing you would check on a site that is invisible in AI answers?
items.summary_html:
Many business sites look fine to people but are hard for search engines and AI tools to read. Here is a short checklist you can run in about 15 minutes.

  1. Can crawlers get in? Open yourdomain.com/robots.txt. Make sure it does not block Googlebot or the AI crawlers you want (GPTBot, PerplexityBot, ClaudeBot).
  2. Is there a sitemap? Open yourdomain.com/sitemap.xml. It should list your real pages and nothing broken.
  3. Does each page have one clear title and one H1 that say what the page is about?
  4. Do your answers appear as plain text near the top of the page? AI tools quote short direct answers, so put the answer first and the detail after.
  5. Do you have basic structured data (Organization, and FAQ where it fits)? Test it with Google's Rich Results Test.
  6. Is the page fast and readable on a phone? Run PageSpeed Insights.
  7. Is your business name, site and contact the same everywhere you are listed?

Fix these in order. None of them needs a big budget. They just need someone to check.

We are Liftup Technologies, a team of 10 in Pune that has worked on websites, SEO and automation since 2015. We built a free tool that checks the AI side of this: https://liftup.tech/tools/ai-visibility-checker/

What is the first thing you would check on a site that is invisible in AI answers?

items.title: From Manual Ticketing to Digital Booking, Solving Bangladesh's Ship Travel Challenges
items.summary: Bangladesh has a transportation ecosystem built around buses, trains, ferries, launches, and ships. Millions of people travel across the country every year, and water transportation remains an important part of both everyday mobility and tourism. Yet booking a ship ticket can still be a surprisingly fragmented experience. A traveler planning a trip to Saint Martin's Island, for example, may need to search multiple Facebook pages, contact ticket agents through WhatsApp, compare fares manually, confirm departure schedules over phone calls, and figure out payment procedures before securing a seat. The process often involves navigating information scattered across different digital and offline channels. This is not simply a user experience problem. It is a technology problem involving information architecture, data consistency, transaction management, customer communication, and the challenges of digitizing a traditionally offline industry. At ShipTickets.bd , we are working to make this experience more accessible by bringing ship ticket information, booking workflows, and customer support into a more structured digital environment. The Problem: A Fragmented Transportation Booking Ecosystem The challenge of booking water transportation in Bangladesh is different from booking a flight or a hotel through a mature global platform. Several factors contribute to the complexity: 1. Information is distributed across multiple channels Passengers often discover ticket prices, seat categories, departure times, and booking policies through different sources. One operator may publish information on Facebook, another may communicate through WhatsApp, and another may rely on physical ticket counters or travel agents. This creates an information gap between travelers and service providers. Passengers have difficulty answering basic questions: Which ships are operating on my travel date? What are the available seat or cabin categories? How much does a ticket actually cost? Is the departure time confirmed? What payment methods are accepted? What happens if the sailing schedule changes? A digital booking platform needs to solve this information fragmentation before it can deliver a meaningful booking experience for St Martin Ship ticket 2. Seasonal demand creates operational complexity Routes such as Cox's Bazar to Saint Martin's Island experience concentrated demand during specific tourism seasons. Demand can fluctuate significantly depending on weather, government regulations, vessel approvals, holidays, and travel restrictions. This means a ticketing system cannot simply display a static product catalog. It must be designed to accommodate changing schedules, pricing, booking conditions, and operational information. 3. Booking is not always a single transaction In many traditional booking workflows, reserving a ticket and issuing a confirmed ticket are two separate operational steps. A passenger may select a seat, submit personal information, make an advance payment, and then wait for payment verification or confirmation from the ticketing operator. From a software engineering perspective, this introduces several states into the booking lifecycle. Treating every booking as immediately confirmed would create inaccurate expectations and potentially operational problems. 4. Trust is part of the technical experience In an emerging online ticketing ecosystem, customers need confidence that the platform is legitimate, their payment has been received, and their booking details are correct. A digital platform must therefore make the booking process transparent, provide clear transaction references, and maintain communication throughout the confirmation process. Technology is not just about making the booking form faster. It is also about reducing uncertainty. Moving From Informal Booking to a Structured Digital Workflow The first step in solving these problems is to transform the booking journey into a structured workflow. Instead of requiring customers to collect information from multiple sources, a booking platform can organize the process into clearly defined steps: Search for a journey by date and destination. Compare available ships and ticket categories. Select a seat, cabin, or ticket type. Enter passenger information. Review the fare and payment requirements. Submit payment information. Receive booking updates and confirmation. This structure creates a predictable user experience while making the underlying booking data easier to manage. At ShipTickets.bd, the objective is to simplify the journey of booking Saint Martin ship tickets by bringing ship options, ticket prices, journey details, and booking information into a centralized online experience. The Technical Foundation: Designing Around the Booking Lifecycle A reliable booking experience starts with understanding that a ticket is more than a product displayed on a webpage. It represents a journey, a passenger, a vessel, a departure date, a ticket category, a payment, and a confirmation process. These relationships should be reflected in the system's data model and business logic. 1. Structured journey and ticket information A booking platform needs a consistent way to represent journeys and ticket options. Conceptually, the system can organize information around entities such as: Route: Origin, destination, and journey direction. Vessel: Ship identity and operator information. Booking submissions should also be protected against accidental duplicate actions. A good user experience communicates what is happening. Some important areas for future development include: Inventory synchronization Connecting booking platforms with operator inventory systems could improve the accuracy of availability information and reduce the need for manual confirmation. However, real-time inventory synchronization requires reliable integrations and cooperation from transportation operators. It should be introduced where the underlying operational systems support it. items.summary_html:
Bangladesh has a transportation ecosystem built around buses, trains, ferries, launches, and ships. Millions of people travel across the country every year, and water transportation remains an important part of both everyday mobility and tourism.

Yet booking a ship ticket can still be a surprisingly fragmented experience.

A traveler planning a trip to Saint Martin's Island, for example, may need to search multiple Facebook pages, contact ticket agents through WhatsApp, compare fares manually, confirm departure schedules over phone calls, and figure out payment procedures before securing a seat. The process often involves navigating information scattered across different digital and offline channels.

This is not simply a user experience problem. It is a technology problem involving information architecture, data consistency, transaction management, customer communication, and the challenges of digitizing a traditionally offline industry.

At ShipTickets.bd, we are working to make this experience more accessible by bringing ship ticket information, booking workflows, and customer support into a more structured digital environment.

The Problem: A Fragmented Transportation Booking Ecosystem

The challenge of booking water transportation in Bangladesh is different from booking a flight or a hotel through a mature global platform.

Several factors contribute to the complexity:

1. Information is distributed across multiple channels

Passengers often discover ticket prices, seat categories, departure times, and booking policies through different sources.

One operator may publish information on Facebook, another may communicate through WhatsApp, and another may rely on physical ticket counters or travel agents.

This creates an information gap between travelers and service providers.

Passengers have difficulty answering basic questions:

  • Which ships are operating on my travel date?
  • What are the available seat or cabin categories?
  • How much does a ticket actually cost?
  • Is the departure time confirmed?
  • What payment methods are accepted?
  • What happens if the sailing schedule changes?

A digital booking platform needs to solve this information fragmentation before it can deliver a meaningful booking experience for St Martin Ship ticket

2. Seasonal demand creates operational complexity

Routes such as Cox's Bazar to Saint Martin's Island experience concentrated demand during specific tourism seasons.

Demand can fluctuate significantly depending on weather, government regulations, vessel approvals, holidays, and travel restrictions.

This means a ticketing system cannot simply display a static product catalog. It must be designed to accommodate changing schedules, pricing, booking conditions, and operational information.

3. Booking is not always a single transaction

In many traditional booking workflows, reserving a ticket and issuing a confirmed ticket are two separate operational steps.

A passenger may select a seat, submit personal information, make an advance payment, and then wait for payment verification or confirmation from the ticketing operator.

From a software engineering perspective, this introduces several states into the booking lifecycle.

Treating every booking as immediately confirmed would create inaccurate expectations and potentially operational problems.

4. Trust is part of the technical experience

In an emerging online ticketing ecosystem, customers need confidence that the platform is legitimate, their payment has been received, and their booking details are correct.

A digital platform must therefore make the booking process transparent, provide clear transaction references, and maintain communication throughout the confirmation process.

Technology is not just about making the booking form faster. It is also about reducing uncertainty.

Moving From Informal Booking to a Structured Digital Workflow

The first step in solving these problems is to transform the booking journey into a structured workflow.

Instead of requiring customers to collect information from multiple sources, a booking platform can organize the process into clearly defined steps:

  1. Search for a journey by date and destination.
  2. Compare available ships and ticket categories.
  3. Select a seat, cabin, or ticket type.
  4. Enter passenger information.
  5. Review the fare and payment requirements.
  6. Submit payment information.
  7. Receive booking updates and confirmation.

This structure creates a predictable user experience while making the underlying booking data easier to manage.

At ShipTickets.bd, the objective is to simplify the journey of booking Saint Martin ship tickets by bringing ship options, ticket prices, journey details, and booking information into a centralized online experience.

The Technical Foundation: Designing Around the Booking Lifecycle

A reliable booking experience starts with understanding that a ticket is more than a product displayed on a webpage.

It represents a journey, a passenger, a vessel, a departure date, a ticket category, a payment, and a confirmation process.

These relationships should be reflected in the system's data model and business logic.

1. Structured journey and ticket information

A booking platform needs a consistent way to represent journeys and ticket options.

Conceptually, the system can organize information around entities such as:

  • Route: Origin, destination, and journey direction.
  • Vessel: Ship identity and operator information.
  • Schedule: Departure and return dates and times.
  • Ticket category: Seat class, cabin type, or other ticket options.
  • Fare: Pricing associated with a journey and ticket category.
  • Passenger: Traveler information required for ticket issuance.
  • Booking: The customer's selected journey and ticket details.
  • Payment: Payment amount, method, and transaction reference.
  • Confirmation: Booking verification and ticket issuance status.

This separation is important because schedules, fares, and ticket categories can change independently.

For example, changing a departure time should not require rewriting passenger information or payment records. Similarly, updating a fare should not affect existing bookings.

A structured data model makes these operations easier to maintain and audit.

2. A booking state machine instead of a simple booking flag

One of the most important architectural decisions in ticketing is how booking status is managed.

A simple boolean field such as booked = true is insufficient for a workflow involving payment verification and ticket issuance.

A more meaningful booking lifecycle could look like this:

INITIATED
    |
    v
PENDING_PAYMENT
    |
    v
PAYMENT_SUBMITTED
    |
    v
PAYMENT_VERIFICATION
    |
    v
CONFIRMED
    |
    v
TICKET_ISSUED

Additional states may be required for cancellation, failed payment, expired bookings, or unavailable inventory.

Each transition should be governed by specific business rules.

For example:

  • A booking cannot be confirmed without payment verification.
  • A ticket cannot be issued before the booking is confirmed.
  • A payment reference should not be reused for multiple bookings.
  • A booking should not be treated as confirmed merely because a payment form was submitted.

Thinking in terms of a state machine helps prevent inconsistent records and makes the system easier to debug.

It also gives customer support teams a clearer view of what happened when a customer reports a problem.

3. Payment verification and transaction integrity

Digital payment integration is one of the most sensitive components of an online ticketing platform.

In Bangladesh, payment methods such as bKash and bank transfers are familiar to customers. However, accepting a payment reference is not the same as verifying a payment.

A robust payment workflow should distinguish between:

  • Payment initiated by the customer.
  • Transaction reference submitted.
  • Payment received.
  • Payment verified.
  • Payment associated with the correct booking.
  • Booking confirmed.

Transaction references should be validated against the booking context, and duplicate submissions should be handled carefully.

Idempotency is particularly important in payment-related workflows. If a customer submits the same transaction reference multiple times because of a network interruption or repeated form submission, the system should avoid processing the same payment more than once.

Even when payment verification involves an operational team, the digital system should maintain a clear record of the verification process.

This creates a foundation for future automation without compromising the reliability of the current workflow.

Designing for Real-World Constraints

Software built for Bangladesh needs to account for the way people actually access digital services.

A technically sophisticated application can still fail if it performs poorly on slower connections, creates unnecessary data entry requirements, or assumes that every user is comfortable navigating complex interfaces.

Mobile-first architecture

Many customers access travel services through smartphones.

A booking interface should therefore prioritize:

  • Responsive layouts across different screen sizes.
  • Lightweight pages and optimized images.
  • Minimal unnecessary navigation.
  • Clear forms with appropriate input types.
  • Easy-to-read fares and booking summaries.
  • Accessible buttons and interaction states.

The objective is to minimize the number of steps required to complete a booking without sacrificing the information customers need to make informed decisions.

Resilient user interactions

Network interruptions are common in real-world mobile environments.

The system should avoid losing customer input when a page reloads or a request fails. Booking submissions should also be protected against accidental duplicate actions.

A good user experience communicates what is happening.

Instead of leaving a customer uncertain after clicking a payment or booking button, the interface should clearly indicate whether the request is processing, has succeeded, or requires another action.

Data validation

Passenger names, mobile numbers, travel dates, and payment references are important booking fields.

Validation should happen at both the client and server levels.

Client-side validation improves usability by identifying obvious errors immediately. Server-side validation ensures that submitted information meets the system's rules regardless of how the request was made.

This distinction is particularly important for booking and payment systems, where the frontend cannot be treated as a trusted source of information.

Connecting Digital Convenience With Human Support

Automation is valuable, but transportation booking in Bangladesh still benefits from accessible human support.

Customers may have questions about ticket categories, travel policies, departure schedules, payment procedures, or changes caused by weather and operational conditions.

Rather than treating customer support as a separate activity, a modern booking platform should integrate it into the customer journey.

At ShipTickets.bd, customers can access booking assistance through WhatsApp and phone support.

This hybrid approach combines the convenience of online booking with the flexibility of human assistance when a situation requires clarification or manual verification.

From a technology perspective, the goal is to keep customer support connected to the booking context.

A support representative should be able to understand which journey the customer selected, what information was submitted, and what stage the booking has reached.

This reduces repetitive communication and makes the resolution process more efficient.

Building for Scalability and Future Improvements

The long-term opportunity for digital ship ticketing extends beyond a single route or tourism season like Tripzic Group trip booking Platform

A scalable booking platform should be able to accommodate additional routes, operators, ticket categories, and operational requirements without fundamentally redesigning the application.

Some important areas for future development include:

Inventory synchronization

Connecting booking platforms with operator inventory systems could improve the accuracy of availability information and reduce the need for manual confirmation.

However, real-time inventory synchronization requires reliable integrations and cooperation from transportation operators. It should be introduced where the underlying operational systems support it.

Automated payment reconciliation

Integrating payment gateways or financial APIs can reduce manual payment verification and improve transaction processing efficiency.

Notification infrastructure

Automated notifications through SMS, email, or messaging platforms can keep customers informed about booking status, payment confirmation, ticket issuance, and schedule changes.

Analytics and operational insights

Structured booking data can help identify demand patterns, popular departure dates, preferred ticket categories, and customer behavior.

These insights can support better planning for both ticketing platforms and transportation operators.

API-driven architecture

As the ecosystem evolves, well-defined APIs can make it easier to integrate booking platforms with operators, payment providers, travel services, and other digital platforms.

The goal is not to introduce complexity prematurely. It is to establish a foundation that supports future integrations when they become operationally useful.

The Bigger Picture: Digitizing Transportation, One Workflow at a Time

The digital transformation of transportation in Bangladesh is not going to happen through a single application or technology.

It requires better information, more consistent operational processes, reliable digital payments, improved communication, and systems that are designed around the realities of local customers and service providers.

ShipTickets.bd is part of this broader effort to make ship ticket booking more accessible and organized.

By bringing journey information, ticket options, booking workflows, and customer assistance into a centralized digital platform, we aim to reduce the friction travelers experience when planning water-based journeys.

The engineering challenge is not simply to build an online ticket form.

It is to create a reliable digital workflow around a complex real-world transportation service — one that can handle changing schedules, payment verification, customer expectations, and operational constraints while remaining simple enough for everyday users.

That is where the real value of technology lies: not in adding complexity to an existing process, but in making the process easier, more transparent, and more dependable for everyone involved.

items.title: SID AI Releases SID-2 Agentic Search Model With 0.720 NDCG Swarm Mode
items.summary: SID AI has released SID-2 , its second-generation agentic search model, alongside SID-2 Swarm. SID-2 is an agentic search model from SID AI that searches your data, reads results and returns ranked document IDs. It replaces fixed RAG pipelines with a model that decides what to search next. TL;DR Size: Context window is 262k tokens per the report (256k on sid.ai/models ). Runs on: Hosted API at platform.sid.ai , plus Baseten and SageMaker reference paths. SID’s latency figures assume 1 B200 GPU at 8 concurrent queries. Performance: A single agent matches Claude Opus 5.5 on retrieval quality. Swarms beat every model SID tested. Best: SID-2 Swarm (12 agents) scores 0.720 NDCG , above GPT-6 Astra at 0.704. Worst: SID-2 Low scores 0.556 NDCG , 0.148 below GPT-6 Astra. Astra still leads on California law, SEC filings and FiQA. Bottom line: Best: frontier-level retrieval at a fraction of the latency. Worst: no disclosed size, weights or independent evals yet. What is SID-2 and how does it work? SID-2 is a small search specialist, not a general chat model. A static pipeline runs rewrite, embed, search and rerank in a fixed order. SID-2 instead searches, reads results, adapts and searches again . Developers implement the search tools against their own backend. A text_search tool covers keyword search and a search tool covers vector search. The model ends each episode by calling report_helpful_ids with a ranked list. No reindexing or data movement is required , since SID-2 only sees what your tools return. SID-2 Swarm runs several agents that message each other and fork their context into new agents. Each agent explores a separate slice of the corpus. SID argues search gains more from reading more documents than from reasoning harder about each one. What are reasoning effort and Metric Steering? SID-2 offers low, medium and high reasoning effort. Each level was trained as a separate expert, then merged with multi-teacher on-policy distillation. Metric Steering lets users target NDCG, F1 or Recall@k, with k from 1 to 50. On SID’s 506-question validation set, SID-2 at high effort scores 0.14 to 0.22 higher per metric than the base model. How was SID-2 trained? Training used 2-stage reinforcement learning. Stage 1 optimizes retrieval quality only. Stage 2 adds a multiplicative latency penalty that applies only to positive rewards. A proposer-solver self-play loop generated hard queries against a frozen SID-1 solver. SID reports a 6x training-throughput gain over SLIME’s default setup. How does SID-2 perform on benchmarks? SID built a 506-question benchmark across 19 corpora. These include HotpotQA, Enron emails, SEC filings, PubMed and BrowseComp-Plus. All numbers below are self-reported from Tables 2 to 4 of the report . SID-2 Medium: 0.585 NDCG in 3.11 s, versus Claude Opus 5.5 (medium) at 0.577 in 25.1 s. SID-2 Swarm, 6 agents: 0.701 NDCG in 17.7 s, versus GPT-6 Astra (max) at 0.704 in 135 s. SID-2 Swarm, 12 agents: 0.720 NDCG, the highest score in the table. Baselines: BM25 scores 0.260 and vector search plus reranker scores 0.287. Swarm leads on 11 of 19 corpora. On WixQA, a single high-effort agent matches Astra at about 232x lower cost. At its lowest effort, SID-2 beats 4 parallel SID-1 runs with 13x fewer FLOPs. && SID-2 vs GPT-6 Astra vs Claude Opus 5.5 Feature SID-2 (medium) SID-2 Swarm (6 agents) GPT-6 Astra (max) Claude Opus 5.5 (medium) Type Agentic search model Multi-agent search General LLM General LLM Parameters Not disclosed Not disclosed Not disclosed Not disclosed Context 262k (report) / 256k (site) Effectively infinite (per SID) Not disclosed 1M NDCG, SID benchmark 0.585 0.701 0.704 0.577 Inference time per query 3.11 s 17.7 s 135 s 25.1 s Cost per 1,000 queries $6.54 $263 $2,141 $131 API price (input / output per 1M) $0.25 / $1.00 $0.50 / $2.00 $10 / $50 $4 / $20 NDCG, time and cost rows are measured by SID on its own benchmark. Retrieval backend time is excluded. How can developers deploy SID-2? SID-2 is available through SID’s API and on Baseten . SDKs exist for Python ( sid-sdk ), TypeScript ( @sid-ai/sid-sdk ) and Go ( github.com/sidhq/sid-go ). A SageMaker helper covers AWS deployments. The reference implementation uses the OpenAI client format. SID-2 costs $0.25 per million input tokens and $1.00 per million output tokens . Swarm costs $0.50 and $2.00. Cached input is 10% of the input price. Key Takeaways SID-2 is an RL-trained agentic search model that returns ranked document IDs. SID-2 Medium matches Opus 5.5 retrieval at 0.585 NDCG in 3.11 s. 12-agent SID-2 Swarm leads SID’s benchmark at 0.720 NDCG. Pricing starts at $0.25 per million input tokens, with no reindexing. All results are self-reported; size and weights are undisclosed. Check out the SID-2 technical report , the docs and the model page . items.summary_html:
SID AI has released SID-2, its second-generation agentic search model, alongside SID-2 Swarm. SID-2 is an agentic search model from SID AI that searches your data, reads results and returns ranked document IDs. It replaces fixed RAG pipelines with a model that decides what to search next.

TL;DR
  • Size: Context window is 262k tokens per the report (256k on sid.ai/models).
  • Runs on: Hosted API at platform.sid.ai, plus Baseten and SageMaker reference paths. SID’s latency figures assume 1 B200 GPU at 8 concurrent queries.
  • Performance: A single agent matches Claude Opus 5.5 on retrieval quality. Swarms beat every model SID tested.
  • Best: SID-2 Swarm (12 agents) scores 0.720 NDCG, above GPT-6 Astra at 0.704.
  • Worst: SID-2 Low scores 0.556 NDCG, 0.148 below GPT-6 Astra. Astra still leads on California law, SEC filings and FiQA.
  • Bottom line: Best: frontier-level retrieval at a fraction of the latency. Worst: no disclosed size, weights or independent evals yet.
What is SID-2 and how does it work?

SID-2 is a small search specialist, not a general chat model. A static pipeline runs rewrite, embed, search and rerank in a fixed order. SID-2 instead searches, reads results, adapts and searches again.

Developers implement the search tools against their own backend. A text_search tool covers keyword search and a search tool covers vector search. The model ends each episode by calling report_helpful_ids with a ranked list. No reindexing or data movement is required, since SID-2 only sees what your tools return.

SID-2 Swarm runs several agents that message each other and fork their context into new agents. Each agent explores a separate slice of the corpus. SID argues search gains more from reading more documents than from reasoning harder about each one.

What are reasoning effort and Metric Steering?

SID-2 offers low, medium and high reasoning effort. Each level was trained as a separate expert, then merged with multi-teacher on-policy distillation. Metric Steering lets users target NDCG, F1 or Recall@k, with k from 1 to 50. On SID’s 506-question validation set, SID-2 at high effort scores 0.14 to 0.22 higher per metric than the base model.

How was SID-2 trained?

Training used 2-stage reinforcement learning. Stage 1 optimizes retrieval quality only. Stage 2 adds a multiplicative latency penalty that applies only to positive rewards. A proposer-solver self-play loop generated hard queries against a frozen SID-1 solver. SID reports a 6x training-throughput gain over SLIME’s default setup.

How does SID-2 perform on benchmarks?

SID built a 506-question benchmark across 19 corpora. These include HotpotQA, Enron emails, SEC filings, PubMed and BrowseComp-Plus. All numbers below are self-reported from Tables 2 to 4 of the report.

  • SID-2 Medium: 0.585 NDCG in 3.11 s, versus Claude Opus 5.5 (medium) at 0.577 in 25.1 s.
  • SID-2 Swarm, 6 agents: 0.701 NDCG in 17.7 s, versus GPT-6 Astra (max) at 0.704 in 135 s.
  • SID-2 Swarm, 12 agents: 0.720 NDCG, the highest score in the table.
  • Baselines: BM25 scores 0.260 and vector search plus reranker scores 0.287.

Swarm leads on 11 of 19 corpora. On WixQA, a single high-effort agent matches Astra at about 232x lower cost. At its lowest effort, SID-2 beats 4 parallel SID-1 runs with 13x fewer FLOPs.

NDCG, time and cost rows are measured by SID on its own benchmark. Retrieval backend time is excluded.

How can developers deploy SID-2?

SID-2 is available through SID’s API and on Baseten. SDKs exist for Python (sid-sdk), TypeScript (@sid-ai/sid-sdk) and Go (github.com/sidhq/sid-go). A SageMaker helper covers AWS deployments. The reference implementation uses the OpenAI client format.

SID-2 costs $0.25 per million input tokens and $1.00 per million output tokens. Swarm costs $0.50 and $2.00. Cached input is 10% of the input price.

Key Takeaways
  • SID-2 is an RL-trained agentic search model that returns ranked document IDs.
  • SID-2 Medium matches Opus 5.5 retrieval at 0.585 NDCG in 3.11 s.
  • 12-agent SID-2 Swarm leads SID’s benchmark at 0.720 NDCG.
  • Pricing starts at $0.25 per million input tokens, with no reindexing.
  • All results are self-reported; size and weights are undisclosed.

Check out the SID-2 technical report, the docs and the model page. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension.

items.title: Sarvam’s Token Factory Sparks India’s Sovereign AI Debate, Again
items.summary: Sarvam AI seems to have found itself in a familiar position. Every new move by the company seems to reopen a larger debate about India's AI ambitions: should domestic AI companies focus on building indigenous models or on making the world's best models accessible through Indian infrastructure? Its latest launch, Token Factory, has once again exposed the conflicting expectations surrounding India's most prominent AI startup. This time, the debate is not about whether Sarvam has built a genuinely indigenous foundation model, but why a company backed by the IndiaAI Mission is hosting models developed by Chinese AI companies. On November 16, Sarvam launched Token Factory, an inference platform that gives developers and enterprises access to eight AI models through a single OpenAI-compatible API. All the models are hosted on GPU infrastructure in India, allowing customers to run inference without routing requests through overseas providers. The catalogue includes Sarvam’s own 105B model, alongside models from DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM and Google. Pricing starts at ₹14 per million input tokens for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, with Sarvam also offering zero-data-retention options for enterprises. The proposition is commercially straightforward. Instead of building and maintaining expensive GPU infrastructure, developers can access several open-weight models through one provider, with their data remaining in India. But six of the eight models listed are Chinese, while only one is developed by Sarvam. For a startup selected under the IndiaAI Mission to build an indigenous foundation model, the optics are difficult to ignore. Sarvam received a ₹98.68 crore GPU subsidy for 4,096 NVIDIA H100 GPUs and raised $234 million at a $1.5 billion valuation in June. The government-backed support came with expectations that the company would contribute to India's own foundation model capabilities. However, government support for developing indigenous AI capabilities does not necessarily preclude Sarvam from pursuing other commercial opportunities. The larger question is whether its infrastructure business complements its foundation model ambitions or eventually takes precedence over them. The criticism also comes with a history. In May 2025, Sarvam faced considerable backlash after releasing Sarvam-M , a 24-billion-parameter open-weight hybrid language model built on top of Mistral Small. The model supported 10 Indian languages, including Hindi, Bengali, Gujarati, Kannada and Malayalam. Despite its positioning as an important step for Indic AI research, Sarvam-M received just 334 downloads on Hugging Face in its first two days. Investor Deedy Das called the numbers "embarrassing", arguing that there was little audience for incremental work. He compared it with an open-source model developed by two Korean college students that had attracted around 2,00,000 downloads. The criticism extended beyond Sarvam . BharatGen's Param-1, another government-backed foundation model built from scratch, had received just 12 downloads on AIKosh at the time. The episode exposed a difficult problem for India's AI ambitions. Domestic foundation models were expected to compete with global offerings, but the resources, research capabilities and developer ecosystems needed to do so were still developing. At the same time, even incremental progress was being judged against the likes of OpenAI and DeepSeek. Now, with Token Factory, the criticism has taken a different direction. Instead of questioning why Sarvam built on top of a foreign model, people are questioning why it is hosting foreign models at all. Hemant Mohapatra, an investor in Sarvam from Lightspeed Ventures, pushed back against the criticism on X. "Really don't understand why launching a token-factory product is getting so much criticism thrown" at Sarvam, he wrote, acknowledging that he was biased as an investor. He argued that people were underestimating how much global inference providers were making by hosting global, including Chinese, models in India. His argument points to a part of the AI business that often gets overshadowed by foundation model development. Training a model is only one part of the equation. Running it efficiently, reliably and at a competitive price is an entirely different business. Every time a developer or enterprise sends a request to a model, somebody has to provide the computing power to process it. As AI agents and enterprise applications scale, inference could become an important revenue opportunity for companies that can provide the infrastructure at competitive prices. Sarvam is attempting to capture that market by bringing multiple models under one platform while retaining control over where the computation happens. However, it is not the only Indian company pursuing this opportunity. JarvisLabs launched its own Token Factory around two months before Sarvam's announcement and has been working on improving its inference capabilities. The company has since begun comparing its performance against Sarvam's. Atharva Ingle, associated with JarvisLabs, said it benchmarked three open-weight models across both platforms and claimed JarvisLabs was on par with or faster than Sarvam in speed and latency. These are, however, claims made by a competing provider, and performance benchmarks alone do not establish which platform offers a stronger overall proposition. Pricing, throughput, reliability and enterprise support are equally important considerations. This introduces another uncomfortable question for Sarvam. If smaller Indian infrastructure providers can deliver comparable or better inference performance, how much of the advantage comes from its technology, and how much comes from the capital and government support available to it? There is, however, a distinction that much of the criticism appears to overlook. Hosting a Chinese model on Indian GPUs does not make the model Indian. But it allows Indian enterprises to access that model through domestic infrastructure, potentially keeping sensitive data within the country's borders and reducing dependence on overseas inference providers. Sovereign AI does not necessarily mean developing every model, chip and infrastructure component domestically. A country can also build sovereignty by controlling where its data is processed, how its computing resources are deployed and who provides the services. But that raises a bigger question about what India is actually trying to achieve with its AI investments. If Sarvam can build a profitable inference business by hosting the world’s best models, it could create a sustainable domestic AI infrastructure company. That infrastructure could eventually support its own models and those developed by other Indian researchers. Yet if the company becomes a platform that primarily monetises access to foreign-developed models, the original ambition of building India's own foundation models risks becoming secondary. India has already struggled to generate meaningful adoption for some of its early domestic models. At the same time, its AI infrastructure companies are competing in a market where access to the best models, cheap computing and reliable inference matters more immediately to customers than the nationality of the model developer. Ultimately, Sarvam’s Token Factory may be a sensible business decision. But it also raises a question that extends beyond the company: should a company receiving public support to build India’s AI capabilities be judged primarily by its commercial success, or by how much original AI technology it contributes to the country?

items.title: Anthropic Adds Code Mode to Claude Code: Claude Now Chains Tool Calls in JavaScript
items.summary:
Anthropic has added Code Mode to Claude Code as an experimental, opt-in feature. Claude Code Code Mode is a mode in which Claude writes JavaScript that makes several tool calls in 1 step. It shipped in Claude Code v2.1.323 last week . For developers, it changes how the agent spends round-trips on multi-step work. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . TL;DR Works with: It works with Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5 and Fable 5.2. Runs on: An interactive terminal session on the native build, v2.1.323 or later. Windows needs Git for Windows. Anthropic API or Claude subscription only. Performance: Anthropic publishes no benchmark or token-saving figure for Code Mode. Best: Background code can run for up to 2 hours while you keep talking to Claude. Worst: Code that Claude waits on stops after 10 minutes. No Bedrock, Google Cloud, Foundry, -p , Agent SDK, VS Code or Desktop. Bottom line: Best: related tool calls run as 1 program. Worst: narrow availability and coarser auto-mode review. What is Code Mode in Claude Code? Without Code Mode, Claude requests each Bash, Read or Edit call directly. It reads every result before choosing the next step. With Code Mode, Claude writes a piece of JavaScript, and Claude Code runs it in your session. According to the docs , one piece of code can run commands in parallel. It can feed one result into the next call. It can also return only the output Claude needs to read. Anthropic’s example raises a retry limit. The code finds the file, edits it and runs the tests: Copy Code Copied Use a different Browser const files = await $`rg -l "function retryPolicy" src`.text(); const target = files.trim().split("\n")[0]; await edit(target, "maxAttempts: 3", "maxAttempts: 5"); ({ edited: target, tests: $`npm test -- retryPolicy`.nothrow() }); In the conversation, you see the tool calls, such as the diff. You do not see the code by default. Press Ctrl+O to open the transcript viewer and expand a collapsed Code row. Claude Code Code Mode: interactive explainer
Claude Code v2.1.323+ · Experimental

How Code Mode works

Claude writes JavaScript that makes several tool calls in 1 step. Source: Claude Code docs.

Without Code Mode
Model: request Bash (rg)
Tool runs, result to model
Model: request Edit
Tool runs, result to model
Model: request Bash (npm test)
Tool runs, result to model
With Code Mode
Model: writes 1 JavaScript program
rg finds the file
edit(): maxAttempts 3 to 5
npm test runs
Only path + test output return
Blue dashed = model turn. Clay = tool work.
const files = await $`rg -l "function retryPolicy" src`.text(); const target = files.trim().split("\n")[0]; await edit(target, "maxAttempts: 3", "maxAttempts: 5"); ({ edited: target, tests: $`npm test -- retryPolicy`.nothrow() });

You see the tool calls (such as the diff), not the code. Press Ctrl+O to open the transcript and expand a Code row.

Set the variable
macOS / Linux / WSLPowerShellsettings.json 
CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_CODE_MODE=1 claude
$env:CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_CODE_MODE = "1" claude
// ~/.claude/settings.json { "env": { "CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_CODE_MODE": "1" } }
Steps
  1. Run claude --version; update if older than v2.1.323
  2. Start with the variable set to 1
  3. Pick "Yes, turn on Code Mode"
  4. Give Claude a many-tool-call task
  5. Press Ctrl+O to read the code
A 0 in your shell or settings wins over a 1. Admins can set 0 in managed settings to block it org-wide, but cannot force it on.
Auto modeOther permission modes
Every tool call inside the code still passes your deny and ask rules and PreToolUse hooks under its usual name. To inspect the code, hook the REPL tool and read tool_input.code.
Claude waits for the code10 min max
Code runs in the background (you keep chatting)2 hr max

The 10-minute limit includes time spent at permission prompts. Background runs need a session started in auto or bypassPermissions mode.

Claude Code Code Mode
JS

Built-in tools in the CLI. No published token figure.

Claude API PTC
37%

Python. Avg tokens 43,588 to 27,297 on complex research tasks.

Code execution with MCP
98.7%

150,000 to 2,000 tokens in 1 Anthropic example.

Figures come from different tasks and setups. They are not a head-to-head benchmark. Cloudflare coined "Code Mode" (TypeScript, V8 isolates) on Sept 26, 2025.
Sources: code.claude.com/docs/en/code-mode · anthropic.com/engineering© Marktechpost
" style="width:100%;height:600px;border:0;display:block;background:#141413;border-radius:16px;" loading="lazy"> How do you turn on Code Mode? Set CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_CODE_MODE=1 in your shell, or in the env block of ~/.claude/settings.json . Before the first session, Claude Code asks you to confirm. Select “Yes, turn on Code Mode”. Claude Code then restarts and shows ‘Code Mode (experimental) is on’. A Code Mode session resumes only with the variable still set to 1. Setting 0 anywhere turns it off, even if 1 is set elsewhere. Admins can block it org-wide with a 0 in managed settings . They cannot force it on. When should developers use Code Mode? Anthropic recommends it for tasks with many related tool calls: A change that repeats across many files A search whose results need filtering before Claude reads them Several independent commands that can run at the same time How does Code Mode handle permissions and long-running code? Each tool call inside the code still passes your deny and ask rules. It also passes PreToolUse hooks under the tool’s usual name, such as Bash. Review differs by permission mode: Auto mode: a classifier reviews each piece of code, not each tool call. It cannot see values computed at run time, such as a path from search output. Other modes: code starts without review, and you are prompted per tool call as usual. Hook authors should check each part of a command. A git push can arrive as cd 'app' && git push . To inspect the code itself, match the REPL tool and read tool_input.code . If Claude waits, the code stops after 10 minutes, including time at permission prompts. In the background, it can run for up to 2 hours while you keep chatting. Background runs need a session started in auto or bypassPermissions mode. What are the requirements and limitations? Version: v2.1.323 or later; v2.1.326 or later with agent teams Account: Claude subscription or Console account. Not available through gateways, Amazon Bedrock, Claude Platform on AWS, Google Cloud, or Microsoft Foundry Organization: no HIPAA configuration or zero data retention Surface: interactive terminal only. No -p , Agent SDK, VS Code panel, Desktop app or cloud sessions Blocked settings: API key helper, OpenTelemetry export or DISABLE_TELEMETRY Unavailable features: Remote Control, Claude in Chrome and computer use How does Code Mode compare with other code-first tool calling? Cloudflare coined ‘Code Mode’ on September 26, 2025 . Its Agents SDK turns MCP schemas into a TypeScript API that runs in V8 isolates. Anthropic then published code execution with MCP . In one example, token use fell from 150,000 to 2,000, a 98.7% saving. Its API feature, Programmatic Tool Calling , uses Python. It cut average usage from 43,588 to 27,297 tokens on complex research tasks. Claude Code’s version applies the pattern to the CLI’s own tools. The docs give no token figure. One independent test reported system-tool context of 11.1k tokens with Code Mode versus 24.6k without. Treat that as a single third-party measurement. Opt in with CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_CODE_MODE=1 on v2.1.323 or later. Background code runs up to 2 hours; waiting code stops at 10 minutes. Auto mode reviews the code, not each tool call. Terminal and Anthropic API only: no Bedrock, Google Cloud, SDK or IDE panel. Check out the Code Mode documentation and the Claude Code changelog . You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . Also, feel free to follow us on Twitter and don’t forget to join our 150k+ML SubReddit and Subscribe to our Newsletter . Wait! are you on telegram? now you can join us on telegram as well. How do you turn on Code Mode?

Set CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_CODE_MODE=1 in your shell, or in the env block of ~/.claude/settings.json. Before the first session, Claude Code asks you to confirm. Select “Yes, turn on Code Mode”.

Claude Code then restarts and shows ‘Code Mode (experimental) is on’.

A Code Mode session resumes only with the variable still set to 1. Setting 0 anywhere turns it off, even if 1 is set elsewhere. Admins can block it org-wide with a 0 in managed settings. They cannot force it on.

When should developers use Code Mode?

Anthropic recommends it for tasks with many related tool calls:

  • A change that repeats across many files
  • A search whose results need filtering before Claude reads them
  • Several independent commands that can run at the same time
How does Code Mode handle permissions and long-running code?

Each tool call inside the code still passes your deny and ask rules. It also passes PreToolUse hooks under the tool’s usual name, such as Bash.

Review differs by permission mode:

  • Auto mode: a classifier reviews each piece of code, not each tool call. It cannot see values computed at run time, such as a path from search output.
  • Other modes: code starts without review, and you are prompted per tool call as usual.

Hook authors should check each part of a command. A git push can arrive as cd 'app' && git push. To inspect the code itself, match the REPL tool and read tool_input.code.

If Claude waits, the code stops after 10 minutes, including time at permission prompts. In the background, it can run for up to 2 hours while you keep chatting. Background runs need a session started in auto or bypassPermissions mode.

What are the requirements and limitations?
  • Version: v2.1.323 or later; v2.1.326 or later with agent teams
  • Account: Claude subscription or Console account. Not available through gateways, Amazon Bedrock, Claude Platform on AWS, Google Cloud, or Microsoft Foundry
  • Organization: no HIPAA configuration or zero data retention
  • Surface: interactive terminal only. No -p, Agent SDK, VS Code panel, Desktop app or cloud sessions
  • Blocked settings: API key helper, OpenTelemetry export or DISABLE_TELEMETRY
  • Unavailable features: Remote Control, Claude in Chrome and computer use
How does Code Mode compare with other code-first tool calling?

Cloudflare coined ‘Code Mode’ on September 26, 2025. Its Agents SDK turns MCP schemas into a TypeScript API that runs in V8 isolates.

Anthropic then published code execution with MCP. In one example, token use fell from 150,000 to 2,000, a 98.7% saving. Its API feature, Programmatic Tool Calling, uses Python. It cut average usage from 43,588 to 27,297 tokens on complex research tasks.

Claude Code’s version applies the pattern to the CLI’s own tools. The docs give no token figure. One independent test reported system-tool context of 11.1k tokens with Code Mode versus 24.6k without. Treat that as a single third-party measurement.

  • Auto mode reviews the code, not each tool call.
  • Terminal and Anthropic API only: no Bedrock, Google Cloud, SDK or IDE panel.

items.title: Neysa Deploys AMD GPU Cluster in Mumbai for AI Training and Inference
items.summary: Neysa has deployed an AMD Instinct MI350X GPU cluster in Mumbai through its Tytan bare-metal AI infrastructure platform. The cluster is now operational and will support large language model training, fine-tuning, generative AI and high-throughput inference workloads. The deployment brings together AMD Instinct MI350X GPUs, AMD EPYC processors and the AMD ROCm software ecosystem. Neysa said the cluster was brought online in a single phase, with global customers already having contracted capacity for AI deployments in India. However, the company has not disclosed the number of GPUs, total computing capacity or the value of the customer commitments. The infrastructure is designed to give customers dedicated access to accelerators, along with control over network architecture, storage, deployment models, and service-level requirements. Customers can choose between bare-metal deployments, bare metal with Slurm, or bare metal with Kubernetes. The deployment also expands Neysa's silicon-agnostic infrastructure strategy. Through Tytan, the company allows customers to select accelerator architectures and operating configurations based on their workloads, while Neysa manages cluster deployment and operations. Neysa said the MI350X cluster is intended to serve both Indian enterprises and global AI companies establishing compute capacity in the country. The company also operates Velocis, a managed AI cloud platform that combines GPU compute, orchestration, inference, observability and cost management. "The question for large AI deployments is no longer simply how many GPUs are available. It is whether the infrastructure can be deployed at scale, operated with certainty and configured for the workload," said Sharad Sanghi , Co-Founder and CEO of Neysa. “Neysa Tytan gives AI offtakers control: dedicated bare-metal capacity and the freedom to choose the silicon, architecture and operating model that fit their requirements. With AMD Instinct MI350X on Tytan, we are expanding that choice while delivering the scale global customers need to deploy AI infrastructure in India.” In October, Neysa partnered with ST Telemedia Global Data Centres (STT GDC) to deploy GPU infrastructure supporting up to 9,000 GPUs at the STT Noida 2 facility. The first phase is expected to go live in Q1 2027 and will support AI training and inference through Neysa's Velocis platform. The multi-year arrangement is designed to serve Indian enterprises and global compute customers, with data residency and predictable latency among its stated objectives. In February, Blackstone and co-investors entered into definitive agreements to provide up to $600 million in equity financing to Neysa, with the company planning to raise another $600 million in debt. The funding was intended to support its expansion plans, including deploying more than 20,000 GPUs across India. Neysa's announcement also marks another major step for AMD in scaling its GPU infrastructure in India. In October, Vultr announced plans to deploy 10,000 AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs in a 20 MW AI supercluster in Chennai. The facility is expected to become India's largest AMD Instinct supercluster and the second-largest globally. Vultr has also outlined plans to expand the infrastructure in 2027 with AMD's next-generation MI455X GPUs and Helios rack-scale architecture.
