items.title: MAVE: Reconstructing Editable 3D Blockouts from Film Shots
items.summary: Animated 3D blockouts support previsualization and provide structural conditions for video generation, but manually reconstructing them from reference videos is costly. This limits both their use by creators and the production of paired training data. We introduce MAVEBench, a benchmark of 50 film shots and 416 keyframes for evaluating camera motion, spatial layout, and character blocking. We propose MAVE, a video-to-blockout framework combining Metric observation, Agentic modeling, and evidence-based VErification. It first recovers cameras, human motion, and geometric evidence in a shared metric coordinate system. An agent then constructs an editable environment under constraints from these observations, while programmatic checks report inconsistencies to guide refinement. The outputs are editable Blender scenes and frame-aligned blockout videos. On MAVEBench, MAVE improves overall scores by 27.5-41.1 points across three agents over their corresponding vanilla baselines. With DeepSeek-1017, it achieves a score of 73.2 at an average API cost of only USD 0.054 per shot, outperforming the strongest vanilla baseline while reducing total reconstruction time by 53%. We also construct MAVEData-3K, a dataset of 3,000 blockout-video pairs for model training, and will release it publicly. Creators can change viewpoints and character paths, then render the edited scenes to condition video generation. Code is available at https://github.com/yfChang-cv/MAVE.

items.title: Disagree to Prune: Reallocating Visual Tokens Where a Small VLM Dissents
items.summary: Visual token pruning speeds up large vision-language models (VLMs) by keeping only a part of their visual tokens. Most existing methods improve the ranking of the tokens and then answer every question once with the same budget. With strong rankings, pruning hurts only a few questions, and signals computed on the kept tokens see little of what it removed. We find that, on most of these questions, a small VLM given the full image disagrees with the pruned answer, since it still sees the missing evidence. We propose PRUDENT, which first answers with about half the budget and spends the saved tokens on re-answering the disagreeing questions at twice the budget. We show when such re-answering pays and why the small VLM should read the full image. On 18 benchmarks, PRUDENT outperforms eight existing pruning methods at the same average budget of visual tokens. Its lead widens as the budget tightens, and holds across five InternVL sizes. PRUDENT also has the highest average in two more model families. The disagreement of the small VLM flags most pruning failures of all eight methods, and re-answering on it also improves the two strongest with their own rankings. Other checkers give similar gains, and the extra tokens go where the first pass hurts the answer. These results suggest that identifying which pruned answers are trustworthy provides an additional lever for visual token pruning beyond the ranking of tokens. Code and data are available at https://github.com/LiZaiyuan0619/PRUDENT.

items.title: LeViT-UNet++: Towards Balanced Fine-Grained Details and Context for Efficient Medical Image Segmentation
items.summary: Efficient medical image segmentation is essential for clinical applications requiring fast and accurate delineation, such as surgical navigation, radiation therapy, and real-time image-guided intervention. Despite substantial advances in convolutional neural networks and Transformers, attaining high accuracy under limited computational resources remains difficult, because reducing model complexity often sacrifices fine-grained structural details and global context modeling, yielding an unfavorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off. To address this, we propose LeViT-UNet++, an efficient encoder-decoder architecture that better balances local detail preservation and global context modeling. Specifically, we introduce a Haar Wavelet Multi-Scale Downsampling (HWMD) module that decomposes feature representations into low- and high-frequency components to extract multi-scale structural information, thereby mitigating detail loss during downsampling. We further develop a depthwise convolution-based decoder that integrates multi-scale global representations from Transformer blocks with local spatial features, enabling progressive feature refinement while reducing computational overhead. Evaluated on four benchmarks (Synapse, ACDC, LA2018, and MSD Heart) under both 2D and 3D settings, LeViT-UNet++ achieves competitive accuracy with a compact parameter footprint and fast inference. items.title: Fast and Strong Image Protection against Diffusion Personalization
items.summary: Personalized text-to-image diffusion models can reproduce a person from a handful of photographs. Image protection perturbs each image before publication so that fine-tuning on it fails, but it optimizes every perturbation from scratch, so its cost grows with the number of images. We present the protective diffusion model (PDM), which is trained once and samples the perturbation of a new image over many denoising steps. PDM distills an iterative teacher and is then post-trained with the target residual projection (TRP) loss as a reward, a stronger objective than existing ones. PDM outperforms nine baselines on faces and artworks and nearly matches its teacher at a tenth of the cost.

items.title: Motion-Aware Reward Modeling for Instruction-Guided Video Editing
items.summary: Reward models for instruction-guided video editing can favor temporal consistency at the expense of motion. We study this failure, termed \emph{motion collapse}, using controlled motion-suppression variants of real edits. On VE-Bench, the evaluated composite reward prefers a motion-suppressed candidate in $97\%$ of cases. Learned video rewards and a VLM judge also struggle with mild suppression, while latent optimization and reward-guided fine-tuning exploit this weakness to increase reward as motion declines. A linear probe of our base reward backbone performs near chance on mild suppression, motivating an explicit inter-frame dynamics input. We propose a motion-aware reward model that combines an RGB frame-difference stream with preference training against motion-suppressed and fabricated-motion negatives. A distillation anchor preserves alignment with human quality judgments. On the VE-Bench motion ladder, our model reduces the rate of selecting motion-suppressed candidates to $0\%$ while achieving a Spearman correlation of $0.57$ with human quality ratings. It also detects unseen suppression variants and preserves motion during reward-guided fine-tuning on two editing pipelines. These results support explicitly modeling motion in rewards for video editing.

items.title: Efficient Self-Supervised Adaptation of 3D Abdominal Vision-Language Model for Institution-Specific HCC Classification via Full Fine-Tuning and PEFT
items.summary: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) capture cross-modal relationships between image and text, yet their adaptation to institution-specific clinical tasks remains underexplored. In this study, we fine-tuned a pretrained 3D medical VLM for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) classification using paired abdominal CT scans and radiology reports from a different institution with acquisition characteristics that differ from the model's original pretraining corpus. We compared two adaptation strategies: full fine-tuning and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), motivated by the common use of PEFT to reduce computational cost and enable adaptation under limited-data constraints. Both approaches achieve strong downstream HCC classification performance despite the cross-institutional domain shift, with PEFT reaching an AUC of 0.79 and F1 of 0.70, and full fine-tuning achieving an AUC of 0.82 and F1 of 0.71. Although these results remain below the performance reported by supervised HCC classification approaches, our method achieves improvements over the pretrained model through CT-report contrastive learning without requiring lesion-level annotations or HCC classification labels as training targets. Full fine-tuning converges rapidly but overfits within a few epochs, whereas PEFT (ConvLoRA for the image encoder and LoRA for the text encoder) attains comparable performance while updating approximately 1% of the model parameters, although requiring more training steps. We also examine the role of contrastive temperature, observing that temperature initialization significantly affects classification performance. This study demonstrates that a 3D medical VLM can be efficiently adapted to institution-specific HCC classification using self-supervised CT-report contrastive learning, while highlighting the practical trade-offs between full fine-tuning and parameter-efficient fine-tuning.

items.title: EfficientVPR: Toward Efficient Visual Place Recognition via Scene-Aware Prompt Tuning and Adaptive Feature Enhancement
items.summary: Visual place recognition (VPR) faces critical challenges in handling extreme environmental variations while meeting the computational constraints of practical applications. Current methods predominantly address these challenges by either scaling up model capacity or employing computationally intensive reranking stages, creating a significant efficiency bottleneck. To overcome this limitation, we propose EfficientVPR, a lightweight one-stage framework that achieves speed-accuracy trade-offs through two key innovations: i) a scene-aware visual prompt tuning method which adapts pretrained features with less parameters while dynamically adjusting to sample-specific characteristics, and ii) an instance-dependent key local feature enhancement module that further reinforces discriminative regions. Comprehensive evaluations on Pitts250k, MSLS, Eynsham, AmsterTime and SVOX demonstrate that our method establishes a new SOTA for DINOv2-small models by outperforming all same-scale competitors, and delivers a $73\times$ speedup with 60\% lower-dimensional features while maintaining competitive (within 2.5% average R@1 gap) against the SOTA DINOv2-large-based two-stage method. Our code will be available at https://github.com/WiniTang/EfficientVPR.

items.title: Reliability-Driven Feature Correction for Hyperspectral and LiDAR Classification
items.summary: Hyperspectral image (HSI) and LiDAR data provide complementary spectral and elevation information for land-cover classification. However, the spatially varying class-discriminative reliability of modality features is rarely modeled explicitly, allowing weak or ambiguous features to adversely affect cross-modal interaction and fusion. To address this issue, we propose ReDF, a reliability-driven framework that quantifies the reliability of each modality's features at each spatial location through the strength of class-related evidence they provide, and uses it to guide feature correction and fusion. Specifically, a Reliability-Guided Feature Correction module introduces a class prototype bank for each modality and converts feature-prototype similarities into class evidence for reliability estimation. The estimated reliabilities are used to construct a reliability-weighted shared representation and to guide bidirectional cross-modal feature correction based on neighborhood agreement, refining modality features with weak class evidence through information from the other modality. Building on these outputs, a Reliability-Guided Feature Reweighting module conditions a low-rank modulation on the estimated reliabilities and the cross-modal disagreement, and applies it to the corrected modality-specific descriptors to adaptively rescale each modality's contribution to the fused representation used for final classification. Experiments on three public HSI-LiDAR datasets show higher mean overall accuracy and Kappa than the compared methods.

items.title: ATS: Anti-Aliased Triangle Splatting with Exact Per-Primitive Integrals
items.summary: Triangle Splatting represents scenes using semi-transparent triangles, but it evaluates each triangle at the pixel center and culls any triangle with an inradius smaller than one pixel. The former causes severe aliasing, while the latter culls most of the scene at lower resolutions. We show that the integral of the Triangle Splatting window over a pixel admits an exact closed-form solution. The angle bisectors split the triangle into three sub-triangles, in each of which the window is a power of the distance to one edge. Each piece therefore has a closed-form antiderivative, and Green's theorem reduces the integral and its gradients to one term per side of the sub-triangle clipped against the pixel. The integral over the whole triangle, which we show has a closed form, then allows conservative culling, removing only triangles that cannot meet the renderer's alpha cutoff at any pixel. This exact formulation anti-aliases existing models without retraining, exhibits less temporal aliasing than 2x2 supersampling, and enables multi-scale training, matching or outperforming supersampled training at reduced resolutions.

items.title: From Perception to Simulation: Unveiling and Empowering Mental Spatial Dynamics in MLLMs
items.summary: Spatial reasoning is a fundamental component of world understanding for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). While existing research has advanced the perception of spatial relations in static scenes, the domain of dynamic spatial simulation remains relatively unexplored. To bridge this gap, we introduce MentalGrid, a benchmark focused on spatial reasoning tasks that require models to simulate evolving spatial states without intermediate visual feedback. Extensive evaluation on our benchmark reveals a significant deficiency in the spatial simulation capabilities of existing models. Specifically, we find that performance is constrained by perceptual limitations in simple simulation scenarios and hindered by inadequate multi-step reasoning as complexity increases. To address these challenges, we propose a three-stage curriculum learning framework utilizing 16k specialized spatial reasoning samples. This approach yields SpatialWalker, which achieves a 33.8% average improvement over its base model, surpassing proprietary models like Gemini-3-Flash in spatial simulation. Furthermore, SpatialWalker demonstrates robust generalization, maintaining a 4.9% average gain on out-of-domain benchmarks, demonstrating the pivotal role of spatial simulation as a fundamental building block for broader spatial intelligence.

items.title: Fast Training-Free Low-Light Video Enhancement with a Frozen Image Diffusion Prior
items.summary: Pretrained image diffusion models can enhance low-light video without low-light training data and without retraining for a new camera. ZVRD, the only published training-free method for low-light video, is too slow to use: our implementation needs over a minute per $256 \times 256$ frame. We present a causal, training-free pipeline that adds two temporal components to a frozen MR. Illuminate image prior. Temporal input fusion recursively averages motion-compensated low-light frames before diffusion inversion. Late-start offset propagation runs the full sampling trajectory only on key frames. Each non-key frame inverts the low-noise part of its own trajectory and adds an enhancement offset warped from the latest key frame. At ZVRD's own resolution the pipeline is $261\times$ faster than ZVRD and scores better on all five metrics we report. On 13 held-out SDSD clips at $1280 \times 720$, it improves on framewise eight-step processing by 0.55 dB in PSNR and 0.034 in LPIPS and halves the warping error, in 10% less time. Measurements inside the model show why, and a linear-Gaussian model of inversion explains them. Fusion removes frame-to-frame noise before inversion amplifies it. A flow error perturbs the transported offset ten times less than it perturbs a transported state. The perceptual gain does not transfer to low resolution: at $346 \times 260$, LPIPS is worse by 0.028. At 0.65 frames per second, the pipeline is an offline method.

items.title: Strong Fused Performance Can Mask Branch Collapse in a Dual-View Heart-Sound Classifier: A Three-Part Diagnostic Protocol
items.summary: Fusion models are usually judged by their fused score, a practice that assumes that every branch has learned something useful. We show that this assumption can fail silently in dual-view heart-sound classification. In AudioFuse, which fuses a spectrogram transformer with a waveform CNN, the spectrogram branch is unused despite strong fused performance when both branches are trained from scratch. We introduce a three-part diagnostic for branch collapse: whether deleting a branch changes the fused score, whether a linear probe on its features beats an untrained copy of the same branch, and whether the branch can learn its view when trained alone. Deleting the branch has negligible effect, and probing its features shows little improvement over an identically initialised, untrained copy. Yet the same architecture trained alone exceeds 0.9 AUC, so its view is learnable, while the jointly trained model is near chance when it must rely on this branch. Update statistics and an initialisation experiment point to an early optimisation imbalance. Moving a strong artificial label cue from one input to the other can switch which branch the model relies on, even though the branch architectures stay the same. We observe branch collapse on PhysioNet, but the full diagnostic is not met on ICBHI or CirCor. Fused performance alone therefore cannot establish that every branch learned a meaningful representation, and we recommend reporting branch deletion and an untrained-control probe alongside it.

items.title: Plausible Videos Can Lead to Poor Decisions: Diagnosing and CURE-ing World Models for Planning
items.summary: Action-conditioned world models are increasingly used as world models for planning, yet a world model that makes plausible, realistic-looking videos that are consistent with the training data can produce poor decisions. We address two key questions: (1) when can we trust a world model for planning, and (2) what should we do when we cannot? We introduce CURE (Certify, Upweight, Rollout, Explore), a certificate-guided technique that assesses whether a world model can be trusted for planning and determines what to do next: whether to upweight the training data to debias the model; roll out more samples at test time; or explore by collecting new data where support (how well the training data cover the planner's decisions) is missing. We deploy CURE across multiple domains, spanning simulated physics based on PhyWorld, MuJoCo arm control, and Language-Table pushing in simulation and on real videos. The decisions our certificate trusts have lower regret than those it does not (e.g., 0.06 vs. 0.38 on Language-Table sim and 0.07 vs. 0.38 on MuJoCo contact), whereas video perceptual quality does not identify good decisions. By focusing on decision quality rather than perceptual quality, CURE lowers regret over the best pessimistic decision rule by 10-25% across support levels, and over world-action models, search and policy learning by 41-64%, given the same data.

items.title: Lost in Read-out: Locating the Image Quality Gap in Vision-Language Models with a Closed-Form Edit
items.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) are widely used as zero-shot image quality assessors, yet their good-vs-poor answers agree only moderately with human opinion. We ask whether these models fail to see quality or fail to say it. Layer-wise probes on five VLMs point to the second: quality is linearly decodable from the vision encoder and still from the last language layer, far better than the answer reveals, and about a hundred labels recover most of it. The loss lies mainly in the final read-out, which partly reads something else: relative to human opinion, it over-rewards colorfulness and under-rewards sharpness on all five models. We test this by intervention: if the read-out is at fault, a closed-form edit of a single last-layer neuron, fitted to many prompts at once, should close the gap and no more. Both hold. Under prompts never used for fitting, the edit recovers 86--100\% of what a ridge head on the last-layer state, fitted under the same prompts, finds beyond the answer on KonIQ. Where that gap is small, it gains little, too little for our transfer criterion on the two largest models; where the head itself is below the answer, it lowers the score; and it works only when written from the middle of the language model on. Unlike unconstrained fine-tuning, the edit leaves perception question answering intact. It does not carry over to yes-or-no or rating questions, and it reverses the good--poor contrast after sentiment-laden sentences. Code will be made available.

items.title: Semantic-Guided Geometric Decoding for Token-Efficient Visual Grounding
items.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) provide a unified interface for language-conditioned visual perception. In pixel-to-sequence grounding, autoregressive coordinate generation requires multiple sequential decoding steps per box, increasing inference cost with the number of instances. Pixel-to-embedding methods reduce this overhead but lack explicit spatial encoding when using a shared special token. We introduce SemGeo, a token-efficient visual grounding framework that represents each instance with a single grid token for coarse localization. A geometric decoder reuses visual features and hidden states to recover precise discrete box coordinates in parallel. To train proposal generation and box localization together, we introduce Gaussian soft labels that encode coordinate distances during supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Reinforcement post-training further combines box-set rewards with coordinate supervision on model-generated proposals. This stage trains the language model and geometric decoder on their own predictions to mitigate the mismatch between teacher-forced training and inference. items.title: Distilling World Action Models for Efficient Bimanual Manipulation via Anchored Path Matching
items.summary: World Action Models (WAMs) jointly generate future video and robot actions through iterative denoising. Few-step distillation reduces the number of model evaluations, but its coarse updates can move the student away from the teacher's trajectory. We propose Anchored Path Matching (APM), which supervises endpoint and short-transition predictions from states reached by the student. From each state, we continue the teacher to zero noise and use its endpoint and first intermediate state as targets. Modality-routed adapters learn to match both targets from the same starting state. When the two gradients conflict, anchor-priority updates preserve the endpoint gradient and remove the opposing component of the local gradient within each modality. One checkpoint supports 1-, 2-, and 4-step joint generation. The sampling budget can be chosen at deployment without retraining or teacher queries. On RoboTwin 2.0, we train only on Clean demonstrations and evaluate directly on the domain-randomized Random setting. At one step, APM improves closed-loop success over continued base distillation at matched inference budgets by 2.0 percentage points on Clean and 1.4 on Random. Video peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) rises from 30.169 to 32.317 dB, with gains in structural similarity (SSIM) and learned perceptual image patch similarity (LPIPS). On two real-robot tasks, APM improves success over the one-step teacher and reduces control-cycle latency by $21.3\times$ relative to the eight-step teacher.Project page: https://jialonglong.github.io/Anchored-Path-Matching/.

items.title: Propose with the Gradient, Accept with the Loss: One Hedged Attack for Pixel-Sparse Robustness
items.summary: A pixel-sparse adversary may change a few pixels of an image to any value. Robustness to such attacks is currently measured with an ensemble, sparse-AutoAttack (sAA), because its members fail in different places: sparse projected gradient descent (sPGD) trusts a first-order model that a full pixel change breaks, and sparse random search (Sparse-RS) ignores the gradient even where it is informative. We show that both attacks are local searches, each a proposal distribution plus an acceptance rule, and ask what such a search can learn from the gradient. A Taylor bound says what to measure, and measurements at the states the search visits give five rules. The sign of the gradient is its most reliable use at a single pixel and sets a new pixel's value. Its ranking of candidate pixels should be followed loosely, and its ranking of the pixels to remove, which is often more reliable, can be followed more closely. A pixel should not be proposed twice before a move is accepted, and acceptance should be decided by the loss alone. These rules define Gradient-guided Random Search (GRS), which runs once and costs one forward and one backward pass per step. On 13 CIFAR-10 configurations and 5 ImageNet models, GRS matches or beats the best single member of sAA and is within one point of sAA itself or stronger on 17 of 18 settings, and it is significantly stronger than sAA on 8. It uses 3 instead of up to 7 forward-pass units, and on CIFAR-10 it runs 3.7 to 5.0 times faster than the members of sAA run in full.

items.title: PlaceTally: A Test-Time Memory Model for Constructing Place Graphs
items.summary: Counting distinct objects in a video is hard when the camera returns to places it has seen. A vision-language model that reads the whole video answers with a few small numbers, and one that reads it in parts counts an object again in every part that shows it. Object trackers need the category before the video is read, or a fixed vocabulary. We observe that a memory for counting does not need to know what it is looking for, only where it has been: objects rarely leave a room between visits, so parts of a video grouped by place share almost no objects, and a place can be recognised before any question is asked. Building on this, we introduce PlaceTally, a question-blind test-time memory model that constructs a place graph for each video. Each video fragment joins the place of its best earlier match or opens a new place, because a strong match is rarely wrong while a true return often matches weakly. A frozen vision-language model counts each place once from at most 128 of its frames, so every read has a bounded input and the memory grows with the number of places; the graph is built 15 times faster than real time. On RevisitCount, our benchmark of real room re-recordings, it scores 62.5% mean relative accuracy on test rooms and 61.2% on held-out rooms, against 51.2% and 44.3% for the same model reading the whole video. It stays level as rooms return more or less often, while a fixed correction of summed visits moves from 38.5% to 61.4%.

items.title: Sub-Meter Canopy Height Synthesis from Sentinel-2 via Anchored Residual Flow
items.summary: Canopy height models (CHMs) - per-pixel maps of vegetation top height - are essential for forest carbon accounting, wildfire fuel mapping, and tree-level ecology, yet sub-meter CHMs require airborne LiDAR refreshed on multi-year national cycles. We produce 0.5 m CHMs from free 10 m Sentinel-2 imagery, a 20$\times$ cross-modal super-resolution task where optical reflectance must predict geometric height it does not directly observe. Motivated by the perception-distortion trade-off, we derive two operating points with shared conditioning. A deterministic regressor (Anchor) targets low distortion; a conditional flow matching model, trained on the Anchor's residual in a learned CHM latent space (AR-flow), targets perceptual fidelity. Trained on 197k LiDAR-paired tiles spanning 69 ecoregions across the contiguous United States and evaluated on 2,530 held-out tiles against eight baselines, the Anchor achieves 2.83 m MAE using only free satellite input. The AR-flow reduces sliced Wasserstein distance from the Anchor's 1.13 to 0.208, at a higher MAE of 3.68 m. Crown-scale statistics improve, but strict individual-tree detection remains weak: generated sub-pixel detail represents plausible structure rather than measured individual trees. Quarterly continental refresh becomes tractable, letting satellite monitoring inform timing and extent for more expensive data acquisitions.

items.title: Helping AI text detectors keep up with changing conditions
items.summary: A teacher who believes a student’s term paper may have been written by a large language model (LLM) can use a tool for detecting artificial intelligence-generated text to help confirm their suspicions. But the teacher may want to think twice before putting all their trust in the detector. Researchers from MIT and Cornell University showed that such detection tools, which are AI models themselves, can be fooled by AI-generated text disguised to appear as if it were written by a human. Detectors can also fail to identify AI text due to natural shifts in writing habits over time or the emergence of new LLMs. In a new paper , the researchers demonstrated how a special training technique makes an AI detector more accurate and resilient to deception, even as human and AI writing constantly changes. They employed a method called test-time adaptation, which allows a deployed detection model to learn from new, unlabeled data by adjusting its inner workings on the fly. In this way, the model adapts to unseen inputs without being retrained from scratch. In experiments, a commercial detector could only identify about 27 percent of AI-generated text that had been disguised, while the new approach achieved 93 percent accuracy. This method could help educators, editors, publishers, and hiring managers flag LLM-generated writing that people try to pass off as human-written. It could also be used by cybersecurity experts to prevent email phishing scams or identify search engine optimization fraud. “There are many high-stakes contexts where people really care about the identity of the author, from scientific publishing to short story competitions. We’ve shown that test-time adaptation allows your AI detector to be much more robust, even with continual adversarial behavior by AI users,” says study co-author Manish Raghavan, the Drew Houston (2005) Career Development Professor at the MIT Sloan School of Management, who also holds an MIT Schwarzman College of Computing shared position in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS), and is a principal investigator in the Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems (LIDS). He is joined on the paper by lead author Kevin Ren, graduate student at Cornell Tech, and senior author Nikhil Garg, an assistant professor at Cornell Tech. The research will be presented at the Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems. Duping the detectors The proliferation of LLMs that generate human-like text has led to a plethora of commercial AI-detection tools to help people identify whether a piece of writing was authored by a human. But these detection tools can fail when the text they evaluate significantly differs from the text they were taught to identify. This is known as a distribution shift. Detector developers typically train their models by gathering text from the internet that they know to be either AI- or human-generated. They train the model to tell the difference. However, once the detector is released, people might change the way they write or the way they use AI to generate text. For instance, a human in 2030 may write about different topics using new analogies that weren’t common for someone writing in 2010. A detector trained with 2010 data might be unfamiliar with this new writing style and incorrectly mark human-written text as AI-generated. The release of a detection model also creates a cat-and-mouse game between its developers and users who want to bypass it. These individuals can run AI-generated text through an automated “humanizer” software tool that modifies it to appear human-written to the detector. “After the company releases a model, a bunch of ‘humanizers’ pop up to try to beat it, so the company tries to incorporate this humanized text into their training so the detector can identify it, and so on. It’s like rinse-and-repeat. The cycle can go on forever,” says Ren. The researchers explored whether test-time adaptation (TTA) can make an AI detector resilient to these distribution shifts. Adaptation in action In TTA, instead of freezing the model so it can’t change during deployment, researchers allow that model to adapt itself to incoming data after it has been released. For an AI text detector, these data are new pieces of text uploaded by users. These data are unlabeled, so the detector developers don’t know which data were written by humans versus AI models. But these new data represent contemporary human and AI writing — exactly what the developers want the model to be able to predict. With enough examples, the detector learns to identify patterns to determine which data are AI-generated and which are human-generated. The researchers studied TTA by creating datasets to contain a certain amount of AI-generated and human-generated text, but they don’t provide those labels to the model. They also used LLMs to generate some examples that resemble text written by AI to specifically evade a detector. Then they performed the TTA training process and tested the model on ground-truth data. In experiments designed to mimic the natural shift in human language over time, a detector that used TTA was 85 percent accurate, while traditional methods only achieved 73 percent accuracy. And when it came to writing designed to thwart detection tools, existing methods could only identify about 27 percent, while TTA enabled the model to catch more than 93 percent of disguised text. “TTA has the potential to really help deployed AI-detection models in terms of being able to proactively address this iterative ‘gaming’ behavior by adversarial AI users,” Ren says. Adapting to shifts in human writing behavior is a more difficult TTA problem, since the shifts are slower and occur in more subtle ways, he adds. The researchers caution that TTA may not always be an effective solution as future LLMs produce more natural-sounding language and it becomes harder to find verifiable human text to use for training. “It isn’t entirely clear if this will be a solvable problem,” Raghavan says. “There are some big, open questions about how you should think about science, writing, and art in a world where it is infeasible to tell the difference between human-generated content and AI content.” In the future, the researchers want to explore similar strategic domains where TTA could be useful and build better benchmarking tools to help engineers improve these AI detection models in a dynamic fashion. This project used API credits provided by Pangram to use their AI text detectors.

items.title: Nvidia’s First Earnings Report After Huang: $115.8B in Revenue and a Succession Question Investors Can’t Price
items.summary: Nvidia reported $115.8 billion in quarterly revenue on November 17, up 103% from a year earlier, and its board chair told analysts on the same call that the board would not discuss the circumstances of Jensen Huang’s resignation. It was Nvidia’s first earnings report since Huang resigned as CEO on November 12, and the company has no permanent successor. A Record Quarter From Huang’s Tenure The quarter ended October 25, 18 days before Huang resigned, so the results belong to his tenure. Revenue of $115.8 billion beat Nvidia’s own forecast of $108 billion, give or take 2%, by about $7.8 billion. It also cleared the $109.1 billion average estimate compiled by LSEG, according to Fox Business . Data Center revenue reached $107.6 billion, up 110% from a year earlier, according to Nvidia’s earnings release . The segment accounted for about 93% of total revenue. On the earnings call , interim CEO Colette Kress said the Vera Rubin platform generated nearly $20 billion in its first quarter of production shipments, and that hyperscale revenue of $60 billion grew 23% from the previous quarter. Nvidia shares rose roughly 2% in after-hours trading. The $130 Billion Forecast Includes an Extra Week Nvidia guided fourth-quarter revenue to $130 billion, plus or minus 3%, above an LSEG consensus of about $125 billion. The quarter runs 14 weeks instead of the usual 13, a detail the release states in a single clause. Spread across 14 weeks, the midpoint works out to about $9.3 billion a week, against roughly $8.9 billion a week in the third quarter. Weekly revenue rises about 4%, well short of the 12% the headline figures imply. Gross margin is the other number to watch. Nvidia guided it to a range of 71.0% to 72.0%, down from 74.8% on a GAAP basis in the third quarter. The forecast also assumes no Data Center compute revenue from China. What Nvidia Has and Hasn’t Said About Huang’s Exit Nvidia’s November 12 announcement said Huang resigned as president, CEO and board member, effective immediately, and gave no reason. Press reports supply the context. Huang acknowledged an extramarital affair in a November 8 memo to employees, after The Wall Street Journal reported in late October that intelligence officials in the US, Singapore and Taiwan had reason to believe a woman close to him might be a Chinese spy, according to an ABC News timeline . China’s Foreign Ministry called the claim “completely groundless.” The board retained the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to investigate whether Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort and whether company secrets or national security were compromised, CNBC reported . When it announced the inquiry, the board said it had no reason to believe either had been compromised. The investigation is ongoing and its findings are not public. Harvey Jones, who became Nvidia’s first-ever board chair on November 12, said on the call that the board will communicate further “when appropriate.” Kress, Nvidia’s CFO since 2013, is interim CEO and keeps her CFO role until the board names a permanent successor. The board said it will consider internal and external candidates, and Jones said it has retained Heidrick & Struggles to lead the search. The Financial Times reported on November 13, citing people familiar with the matter, that the board had approached Arm CEO Rene Haas, one of several candidates. Arm declined to comment , Reuters reported. On November 17, hours before the call, Huang made his first public statement since resigning. He said he “would be honored” to return if the board decided it served shareholders and employees, and that he is committed to cooperating with the investigation, according to the Korea Times . Jones said on the call that the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” He also said the board will not rush to name a replacement before it finds the right person. Employee sentiment is a separate variable. Reuters, citing Wired , reported that an internal post urging the board to weigh employee views drew more than 1,600 comments, several of them urging Huang’s return. Kress closed the earnings call by telling investors that customers and partners are with Nvidia and that employees are committed. She said Nvidia will remain disciplined in how it commits capital. On the leadership transition, she said that from a business perspective it is “business as usual,” and that Nvidia has spoken with its customers, suppliers and partners. The implication is that the next round of decisions on supply, leases and guarantees will be made under governance Nvidia has not had in its 33 years: an interim CEO who also serves as CFO, and a board chaired for the first time. The commitments are the part a successor inherits, since multi-year purchase and lease obligations of this size will still be in force when the search ends. The fourth-quarter report will show whether the $130 billion forecast holds. The board’s timetable is harder to read: Jones said it will not rush the CEO search, and the board has promised only to communicate on the investigation when appropriate. Until it says more, investors have a forecast to model and no way to put a date or a number on the question behind it.

Nvidia reported $115.8 billion in quarterly revenue on November 17, up 103% from a year earlier, and its board chair told analysts on the same call that the board would not discuss the circumstances of Jensen Huang’s resignation. It was Nvidia’s first earnings report since Huang resigned as CEO on November 12, and the company has no permanent successor.

A Record Quarter From Huang’s Tenure

The quarter ended October 25, 18 days before Huang resigned, so the results belong to his tenure. Revenue of $115.8 billion beat Nvidia’s own forecast of $108 billion, give or take 2%, by about $7.8 billion. It also cleared the $109.1 billion average estimate compiled by LSEG, according to Fox Business.

Data Center revenue reached $107.6 billion, up 110% from a year earlier, according to Nvidia’s earnings release. The segment accounted for about 93% of total revenue. On the earnings call, interim CEO Colette Kress said the Vera Rubin platform generated nearly $20 billion in its first quarter of production shipments, and that hyperscale revenue of $60 billion grew 23% from the previous quarter. Nvidia shares rose roughly 2% in after-hours trading.

The $130 Billion Forecast Includes an Extra Week

Nvidia guided fourth-quarter revenue to $130 billion, plus or minus 3%, above an LSEG consensus of about $125 billion. The quarter runs 14 weeks instead of the usual 13, a detail the release states in a single clause. Spread across 14 weeks, the midpoint works out to about $9.3 billion a week, against roughly $8.9 billion a week in the third quarter. Weekly revenue rises about 4%, well short of the 12% the headline figures imply.

Gross margin is the other number to watch. Nvidia guided it to a range of 71.0% to 72.0%, down from 74.8% on a GAAP basis in the third quarter. The forecast also assumes no Data Center compute revenue from China.

What Nvidia Has and Hasn’t Said About Huang’s Exit

Nvidia’s November 12 announcement said Huang resigned as president, CEO and board member, effective immediately, and gave no reason. Press reports supply the context. Huang acknowledged an extramarital affair in a November 8 memo to employees, after The Wall Street Journal reported in late October that intelligence officials in the US, Singapore and Taiwan had reason to believe a woman close to him might be a Chinese spy, according to an ABC News timeline. China’s Foreign Ministry called the claim “completely groundless.”

The board retained the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to investigate whether Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort and whether company secrets or national security were compromised, CNBC reported. When it announced the inquiry, the board said it had no reason to believe either had been compromised. The investigation is ongoing and its findings are not public. Harvey Jones, who became Nvidia’s first-ever board chair on November 12, said on the call that the board will communicate further “when appropriate.”

Kress, Nvidia’s CFO since 2013, is interim CEO and keeps her CFO role until the board names a permanent successor. The board said it will consider internal and external candidates, and Jones said it has retained Heidrick & Struggles to lead the search. The Financial Times reported on November 13, citing people familiar with the matter, that the board had approached Arm CEO Rene Haas, one of several candidates. Arm declined to comment, Reuters reported.

On November 17, hours before the call, Huang made his first public statement since resigning. He said he “would be honored” to return if the board decided it served shareholders and employees, and that he is committed to cooperating with the investigation, according to the Korea Times. Jones said on the call that the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” He also said the board will not rush to name a replacement before it finds the right person.

Employee sentiment is a separate variable. Reuters, citing Wired, reported that an internal post urging the board to weigh employee views drew more than 1,600 comments, several of them urging Huang’s return. Kress closed the earnings call by telling investors that customers and partners are with Nvidia and that employees are committed.

Purchase Commitments Reach $390 Billion

Kress told analysts that Nvidia’s purchase commitments rose to $390 billion in the third quarter, its data center lease and cloud service commitments rose to a little over $100 billion, and its guarantees totaled $118 billion. She said Nvidia will remain disciplined in how it commits capital. On the leadership transition, she said that from a business perspective it is “business as usual,” and that Nvidia has spoken with its customers, suppliers and partners.

The implication is that the next round of decisions on supply, leases and guarantees will be made under governance Nvidia has not had in its 33 years: an interim CEO who also serves as CFO, and a board chaired for the first time. A new National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee, created November 17 and chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson, now receives reports from Nvidia’s national security and global trade compliance teams. Nvidia’s own release names the risk. It lists the leadership transition and the search for a new CEO among the factors that could cause results to differ from its forecasts, along with the “scope, timing and outcome” of investigations.

The fourth-quarter report will show whether the $130 billion forecast holds. items.title: Why Modern LLMs Don’t Look Like the Original Transformer
items.summary: The familiar diagram had two halves. Follow what changed when the job grew beyond translation. If you’ve ever tried to understand an LLM, you’ve probably come across this picture. It is Figure 1 from Attention Is All You Need , the 2017 paper that introduced the Transformer. There is a lot going on: colored boxes, looping arrows, and two tall stacks that seem to do slightly different versions of the same thing. It is easier to follow once you give the machine a sentence to work on. Suppose we want to translate “The cat is sleeping” into German. The left stack reads the English sentence. The right stack writes “Die Katze schläft.” Now look inside a model such as Llama 3.1 . That separate text encoder on the left is gone. One of the attention blocks on the right has gone with it. If you learned both halves because you wanted to understand chatbots, this can be confusing. The familiar drawing is still a good place to start. We just have to follow what happened after it was published. The left side was there for a reason Look at the arrow that leaves the top of the left stack and crosses into the middle attention block on the right. That connection explains why a translator needs two stacks. The encoder has read the English sentence and built a representation of each token. The decoder can consult those representations while deciding which German token to produce next. When it has written “Die Katze,” it still has access to the English words “is sleeping.” It can use that source information alongside the German text it has already produced. This is the role of cross-attention, the attention between the two stacks. The bottom attention block on the right has another job. It looks at the output written so far. Its mask prevents a position from seeing later output tokens, which would give away the answer during training. So the decoder was already a machine for writing one token after another. The encoder gave it a separate piece of text to consult. That translation story is also where I start in The Translator That Forgot , my visual walkthrough of the paper. Following a sentence through the model makes the arrows much easier to understand than starting with the names of every box. https://medium.com/media/52ff0f612ed6d90a21676b5a11de9e71/href It also makes the next change easier to see. What changed when the model learned to keep writing A translator learns from pairs of texts. Here is the English sentence; here is its German translation. But there is much more ordinary text available than neatly paired examples. Books, webpages and code all contain a different kind of training example: a passage followed by whatever comes next. A model can read a prefix, predict the next token, and learn from whether it was right. Do that across a large corpus, and the same task exposes it to grammar, facts, writing styles and patterns in code. The first GPT paper used a Transformer decoder for this kind of generative pretraining in 2018. Now there is no separate source sentence to encode. The earlier text is already in the same sequence as the text being predicted. A causal attention stack can process that prefix directly. This is the important difference between a decoder-only model and simply covering up the left side of the old picture. The cross-attention block that used to read the encoder’s output goes away too. A chat application can then arrange a conversation as one sequence, using markers to identify the user, assistant and other parts of the exchange. The model continues that sequence with the assistant’s response. Instruction tuning and other post-training help turn a text continuation model into something that follows requests. During training, the text is already available, so the model can process many positions together while masking future tokens. When it generates a new answer, the ordinary autoregressive loop still depends on the tokens it has produced so far. The old encoder has not become useless. A translation model can still use one, and a multimodal model may have a separate image encoder. Its removal from a text-only language model follows from the job that model is being trained to do. Then the conversation got expensive Once a model can continue a conversation, people naturally want it to continue a longer one. They paste a document, ask follow-up questions and expect the earlier details to remain available. For the system serving the model, those earlier tokens have a cost. Attention uses quantities called keys and values to read information from previous tokens. During generation, the system can keep these quantities in a KV cache , saving it from having to recompute them every time it writes another token. Each attention layer keeps its own cache. As the sequence grows, more cached numbers accumulate. Consider an illustrative model with 32 layers, 32 query heads and 128 numbers per head. Suppose it has 8,192 tokens in context and stores each cached number in two bytes. If every query head has its own key and value head, the cache payload is 4 GiB for that one sequence . The model’s weights and other runtime memory are extra. That is a substantial bill for remembering what has already been said. Grouped-query attention , or GQA, changes how that work is shared. Several query heads use the same key and value head. The queries still differ, but the model learns to work with shared keys and values. With eight KV heads instead of 32, the same calculation gives 1 GiB . The arithmetic for the eight-head case is: 2 × 32 layers × 8,192 tokens × 8 KV heads × 128 numbers × 2 bytes = 1,073,741,824 bytes, or 1 GiB. The first 2 counts keys and values. Keep all the other assumptions fixed and multiply the KV heads by four, and you get the 4 GiB case. This saving applies to the cache payload. It does not make the whole model four times smaller or guarantee a fourfold speed-up. And the cache still grows with the sequence: at 32,768 tokens, our eight-head example reaches 4 GiB again. You can see the same pressure behind other designs. DeepSeek-V3’s multi-head latent attention stores a compressed representation of keys and values, along with separate positional information. It takes a different route from GQA, but it is trying to make long histories less expensive to keep. The small boxes changed as well Even after you account for the missing encoder and the smaller cache, a modern block will not match the old diagram box for box. Take position. The order of “dog bites man” matters, even though it contains the same words as “man bites dog.” A model needs a useful way to represent where tokens sit in the sequence. The original Transformer added positional signals to token embeddings. Rotary positional embeddings , usually called RoPE, instead rotate query and key coordinates according to position. The difference between those rotations lets their dot product reflect relative position. That change is useful when working with longer contexts, though extending a model’s context still takes appropriate training, scaling methods and evaluation. The feed-forward box changed too. It transforms each token’s representation after attention has gathered information from other positions. Modern models often use SwiGLU , where a learned gate modulates the values passing through that computation. Then there are the “Add & Norm” boxes. The original drawing puts normalization after each residual sum. Later designs often normalize before the attention or feed-forward computation. Many also use RMSNorm , a simpler rescaling operation that leaves out LayerNorm’s mean subtraction. These names can look like a wall of unrelated acronyms on a model card. Read the Qwen3 architecture description after looking at the old diagram, and they become easier to place. RoPE concerns position. GQA concerns attention heads and their cache. SwiGLU concerns the feed-forward calculation. Pre-RMSNorm concerns how values are normalized before each sublayer. The broad outline is recognizable. The implementation inside it has changed. Some changes were about the GPU There is another reason a modern implementation can look different: the hardware may spend too much time moving intermediate results around. A straightforward attention implementation can write a large matrix of scores to GPU memory, then read it back for the next part of the calculation. The arithmetic might be fast, yet those trips to memory remain expensive. FlashAttention tackles that problem by processing tiles and keeping track of the normalization statistics it needs as it goes. It avoids materializing the full attention matrix in high-bandwidth memory. This is a change in how attention is executed. The operation is still exact dense attention in the mathematical sense, although floating-point execution order can affect numerical results. That distinction matters. GQA changes which heads share keys and values. FlashAttention changes how the GPU carries out the work. You can use both. It also helps explain why “faster attention” does not always mean a new architecture. Dense attention over every position still has quadratic pairwise computation during training or prompt processing. Reading and writing less memory can make that computation much more practical without changing its basic scaling. Others changed how much of the model runs Attention is only part of a Transformer. There are also the feed-forward layers, and these offer another way to increase a model’s capacity. Instead of one feed-forward network handling every token, a mixture-of-experts layer keeps several networks and uses a router to select a few for each token. Qwen3’s MoE variants have 128 experts, with eight activated per token. Its dense variants use a conventional dense feed-forward network. Both remain part of the same architectural family. This lets the model store more capacity without running every expert on every token. It also creates practical problems of its own: experts need to receive useful training, and activations may need to move between devices. The large parameter number on an MoE model therefore tells you how much is stored. The active parameter number tells you more about what participates in processing a token. Neither number, by itself, gives you the full serving cost. The attention mechanism can remain in place throughout this change. The part being reorganized is the feed-forward computation. The next branch looks different again Once you start reading model descriptions this way, you can see where some designs depart further. The official Qwen3.5–35B-A3B model card describes a language backbone that repeats three Gated DeltaNet layers followed by one attention layer. Each layer is paired with MoE, and that four-layer pattern repeats ten times. The DeltaNet layers carry information forward in a recurrent state. The attention layers can access keys and values across the sequence. The designers are combining two ways of handling past information inside one model. Our earlier calculation assumed a full KV cache in every layer. It would not describe the complete state of this hybrid. You have to inspect what each kind of layer actually stores. This model also has a vision encoder. So even the idea that “the encoder disappeared” needs context: a text model can drop the original source-text stack while a multimodal system uses an encoder to process images. There is no single modern diagram that replaces the 2017 one for every LLM. And changes in architecture are only part of the story. Better data, more training and post-training can improve a model substantially while much of its structure stays the same. Meta emphasizes data and scale when explaining Llama 3’s gains. The original picture is still worth spending time with. Look at the arrow between its two stacks, then compare it with a causal language model. Look at the attention boxes, then ask what each layer keeps in memory. The newer designs become easier to understand when you can point to the part that changed. If you want to get comfortable with those attention boxes, the interactive breakdown of Attention Is All You Need works through a query, its scores and the values it gathers. That small calculation gives you something concrete to recognize when you return to a model report. The arrow between the two stacks made sense for a translator. The newer diagrams make sense when you know what their designers were trying to build. Why Modern LLMs Don’t Look Like the Original Transformer was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

The encoder has read the English sentence and built a representation of each token. The decoder can consult those representations while deciding which German token to produce next.

But there is much more ordinary text available than neatly paired examples. Books, webpages and code all contain a different kind of training example: a passage followed by whatever comes next.

A chat application can then arrange a conversation as one sequence, using markers to identify the user, assistant and other parts of the exchange. During training, the text is already available, so the model can process many positions together while masking future tokens. When it generates a new answer, the ordinary autoregressive loop still depends on the tokens it has produced so far.

The old encoder has not become useless. A translation model can still use one, and a multimodal model may have a separate image encoder. Its removal from a text-only language model follows from the job that model is being trained to do.

Then the conversation got expensive

Once a model can continue a conversation, people naturally want it to continue a longer one. They paste a document, ask follow-up questions and expect the earlier details to remain available.

For the system serving the model, those earlier tokens have a cost.

Attention uses quantities called keys and values to read information from previous tokens. During generation, the system can keep these quantities in a KV cache, saving it from having to recompute them every time it writes another token.

This saving applies to the cache payload. It does not make the whole model four times smaller or guarantee a fourfold speed-up. And the cache still grows with the sequence: at 32,768 tokens, our eight-head example reaches 4 GiB again.

You can see the same pressure behind other designs. DeepSeek-V3’s multi-head latent attention stores a compressed representation of keys and values, along with separate positional information. It takes a different route from GQA, but it is trying to make long histories less expensive to keep.

That change is useful when working with longer contexts, though extending a model’s context still takes appropriate training, scaling methods and evaluation.

The feed-forward box changed too. It transforms each token’s representation after attention has gathered information from other positions. Modern models often use SwiGLU, where a learned gate modulates the values passing through that computation.

items.title: Microsoft’s Qubit Now Lasts 20 Seconds. The Hard Question Is Still Open.
items.summary: Majorana 2 is a real materials win. Whether it is a topological qubit will be settled by DARPA’s own tests, not a launch video. Photo by Brecht Corbeel on Unsplash A thousand times better, from a few small changes Microsoft’s Majorana 2 video makes a striking pitch. After 20 years of work on topological quantum computing, the team says it went from Majorana 1 to Majorana 2 in about a year and saw a thousandfold improvement in stability. The changes were in the materials. Majorana 1 used aluminum as its superconductor. Majorana 2 uses lead, and the semiconductor stack now adds antimony to the indium arsenide, grown on a gallium antimonide substrate. In Microsoft’s technical paper, released at Build on June 2, the measured parity lifetime rose from roughly 1 to 12 milliseconds in the aluminum devices to about 22 seconds in the lead device, with some intervals lasting over a minute. The video explains why that matters with simple arithmetic. If an operation takes a microsecond and the qubit’s state lasts a millisecond, you get about one error every thousand operations. If it lasts 20 seconds, you can run tens of millions of operations before a flip. And because that lifetime depends exponentially on the energy gap, modest gains add up fast: the topological gap went from about 30 to about 70 microelectronvolts, and the lifetime went up by more than three orders of magnitude. Microsoft also pulled its target forward. It now expects a scalable, commercially useful quantum computer by 2029, which it says halves its previous timeline. Postquantum’s analysis puts the earlier target at 2033. The consensus: topological quantum computing has arrived If you only watch the video, the story is simple. Theory became reality. Lead was the moment the team saw that what it had predicted actually works. A qubit whose state holds for seconds instead of milliseconds is far more robust, and a machine built from those qubits could reach the chemistry and materials problems no classical computer can solve exactly. The video goes further. Microsoft pitches a loop between quantum and AI: quantum computers produce exact answers about molecules and materials, AI models learn from them, and eventually a Copilot could design materials as easily as it writes an essay. Microsoft also says it used its Microsoft Discovery agentic AI tools to speed up fabrication and measurement, including an agent that found an uncalibrated temperature sensor skewing fabrication data. And there is outside momentum. Microsoft is one of two companies, alongside PsiQuantum, in the final stage of DARPA’s US2QC program, part of its Quantum Benchmarking Initiative. The video addresses skeptics directly. items.summary_html:
Majorana 2 is a real materials win. Whether it is a topological qubit will be settled by DARPA’s own tests, not a launch video.Photo by Brecht Corbeel on UnsplashA thousand times better, from a few small changes

Microsoft’s Majorana 2 video makes a striking pitch. After 20 years of work on topological quantum computing, the team says it went from Majorana 1 to Majorana 2 in about a year and saw a thousandfold improvement in stability.

The changes were in the materials. Majorana 1 used aluminum as its superconductor. Majorana 2 uses lead, and the semiconductor stack now adds antimony to the indium arsenide, grown on a gallium antimonide substrate. In Microsoft’s technical paper, released at Build on June 2, the measured parity lifetime rose from roughly 1 to 12 milliseconds in the aluminum devices to about 22 seconds in the lead device, with some intervals lasting over a minute.

The video explains why that matters with simple arithmetic. If an operation takes a microsecond and the qubit’s state lasts a millisecond, you get about one error every thousand operations. If it lasts 20 seconds, you can run tens of millions of operations before a flip. And because that lifetime depends exponentially on the energy gap, modest gains add up fast: the topological gap went from about 30 to about 70 microelectronvolts, and the lifetime went up by more than three orders of magnitude.

Microsoft also pulled its target forward. It now expects a scalable, commercially useful quantum computer by 2029, which it says halves its previous timeline. Postquantum’s analysis puts the earlier target at 2033.

The consensus: topological quantum computing has arrived

If you only watch the video, the story is simple. Theory became reality. Lead was the moment the team saw that what it had predicted actually works. A qubit whose state holds for seconds instead of milliseconds is far more robust, and a machine built from those qubits could reach the chemistry and materials problems no classical computer can solve exactly.

The video goes further. Microsoft pitches a loop between quantum and AI: quantum computers produce exact answers about molecules and materials, AI models learn from them, and eventually a Copilot could design materials as easily as it writes an essay. Microsoft also says it used its Microsoft Discovery agentic AI tools to speed up fabrication and measurement, including an agent that found an uncalibrated temperature sensor skewing fabrication data.

And there is outside momentum. Microsoft is one of two companies, alongside PsiQuantum, in the final stage of DARPA’s US2QC program, part of its Quantum Benchmarking Initiative.

The video addresses skeptics directly. A researcher in it says skepticism is a healthy part of science and that people who look carefully at the results find them “quite revolutionary.”

That is where the story needs a closer look.

Breaking it: a better material is not yet a proven qubit

Read the paper and the outside analysis, and the picture splits in two.

What Majorana 2 shows is solid materials progress, per Microsoft’s paper as summarized by Postquantum and The Quantum Insider:

  • A parity lifetime of about 22 seconds, measured over 324 intervals in one wire of one tetron.
  • A parent superconducting gap of about 1,300 microelectronvolts with lead, against about 300 with aluminum.
  • A topological gap of about 70 microelectronvolts, against about 30 before.
  • A new radio-frequency method that resolves low-energy states to about 1 microelectronvolt.
Source: Microsoft’s June 2, 2026 paper, as summarized by Microsoft and Postquantum. Values approximate; lifetime measured in one wire of one device; not peer reviewed. Chart by the author.

What it does not show yet:

  • X-basis measurements. The paper reports only Z-parity data. A qubit needs both. Critics argue that a long Z lifetime alone can also come from topologically trivial states.
  • Qubit operations. No gates, entanglement or algorithms are in the paper. Nayak told Science that control and algorithm data exist but are unpublished.
  • The full unit cell. Measurements are on a single wire, not the four-tetron prototype.
  • Independent review. The Quantum Insider notes the paper was not peer reviewed, and there is no data across multiple identical devices.

The history matters here. When Microsoft announced Majorana 1 in February 2025, Nature’s editorial note on the accompanying paper said the results did not represent evidence of Majorana zero modes. This June, Nature published a critique by St Andrews physicist Henry Legg arguing that the plotting code behind Microsoft’s 2025 topological gap results showed only the largest passing region and left others out. Microsoft called it a minor off-by-one-pixel bug, and Chetan Nayak said: “We stand by our results and our roadmap.”

So the same lifetime number reads two ways. To Microsoft, it is protected quantum information. To critics like Legg and Pittsburgh’s Sergey Frolov, the question of whether those states are topological at all has not been answered.

The truth: everyone now says 2029, and DARPA will grade it

Step back and Microsoft’s date stops looking unusual. IBM has said since June 2025 that it will build Starling, a fault-tolerant machine with about 200 logical qubits, by 2029. Quantinuum, which raised about $1.7 billion in its June IPO, has an Apollo system on its roadmap for 2029. Google, which has not named a year, showed in October that magic state cultivation on Willow cut errors about 40-fold, a step toward fault tolerance. 2029 has become the industry’s default answer.

What separates these bets is not the date. It is the kind of evidence behind it. IBM, Google and Quantinuum are scaling qubits that everyone agrees are qubits, and arguing about error rates. Microsoft is betting on a qubit whose basic nature is still disputed, in exchange for a potentially much bigger payoff: if topological protection is real, it could need far less error-correction overhead per useful qubit.

That is why the most important development since the launch is not in the video. In September, Microsoft opened a 15,000-square-foot quantum center at the University of Maryland with a room where DARPA can boot Microsoft’s system and run its own measurements, without Microsoft researchers present, according to Tech Times. DARPA’s evaluators, including teams from four national labs, are looking at exactly the open question: X and Z parity measured on the same device. DARPA’s stated goal is to learn whether any approach can reach utility scale by 2033.

What to watch next:

  1. X and Z on one device. Published, ideally peer-reviewed, data showing both on the same tetron.
  2. DARPA’s verdict. Whether Microsoft stays in the final stage of the Quantum Benchmarking Initiative after on-site testing.
  3. Repeatability. The same lifetime across several nominally identical chips, not one.
  4. Operations, not just lifetimes. Published gate and entanglement data from the multi-tetron unit cell.

One practical note for security teams: Postquantum’s analysis argues that topological qubits do not change near-term timelines for breaking encryption, so post-quantum cryptography plans should stay on schedule either way.

Twenty seconds is an answer to the wrong question, for now

Majorana 2 is a genuine engineering result. Swapping aluminum for lead more than doubled the gap and stretched the measured lifetime from milliseconds to seconds, and the team credits its own AI tools for getting there faster. That deserves attention.

But the question that has followed this program for years is not how long the state lasts. It is what kind of state it is. Until that is answered with data that outsiders can check, Microsoft’s 2029 date rests on a qubit the field has not yet agreed exists.

Microsoft proved its material got better. It has not yet proved its qubit is topological, and that is the only claim the 2029 date depends on.

Sources
  • Microsoft’s Majorana 2 video.
  • Microsoft Source, “Majorana 2, made more reliable with Microsoft Discovery agentic AI” (June 2, 2026), and the paper “20 Second Parity Lifetime in an InAs-Pb Device.”
  • Postquantum, “Microsoft Majorana 2: 20-Second Qubits, Same Questions” (June 3, 2026).
  • The Quantum Insider on Majorana 2 (June 2, 2026), Quantinuum (Aug 12, 2026) and PsiQuantum (July 22, 2026).
  • The Register on Henry Legg’s Nature critique (June 24, 2026).
  • Tech Times on DARPA’s on-site access (Sept 23, 2026).
  • The Block on Google’s magic state result (Oct 16, 2026).
  • IBM’s June 2025 Starling roadmap, as reported by Constellation Research.
