items.summary_html:
What a model is, what training and predicting mean, with a line you fit by dragging points. And why a model does not understand its data. AI course, 0.4.

Note: Although this article can be read independently, it is part of a comprehensive interactive course — the table of contents for which can be found at https://jarroba.com/en/ai-course/—where the entire course is available for free.

“Model”, “train” and “predict” are words that come up constantly when talking about AI, and all three fit in a straight line: the model is the line, training is placing it among the points, and predicting is reading its height at a new point.

Try this first

Open the Regression & MLE tool. You will see ten points and a line that passes between them. The vertical gray lines joining each point to the line are the residuals: how far off the line is at that point. On the right, MSE (loss) is 0.236. MSE is the mean squared error, and loss is the name given to the error you want to make small: each error is squared, the ten are added up and the total is divided by ten. (Further down you have the calculation worked out point by point, in case you want to repeat it on paper.)

Take the fifth point from the left and drag it upward. The line tilts a little toward it and the MSE goes up: the farther you move it, the more. You have not touched the line: it has recalculated itself so that the total error is the smallest possible with the new points. Look also at the equation at the top right, y = 0.687·x + 1.658: while you drag, those two numbers change.

Now click Clear and click in five places on the chart to place your own points. With each click, the line repositions itself. Pay attention to the first three. With one point, the MSE is 0, but infinitely many lines pass through one point and all of them get it right; the tool picks the horizontal one. With two, the line passes exactly through both and the MSE is still 0. From the third on, if they are not aligned, no line passes through all of them and the MSE stops being 0. A line has two numbers to adjust: with two points it always gets it right, even though it has not learned anything.

With three or four points, a red overfitting warning may appear. The tool runs a test: it removes one point, fits the line with the others and checks how much it misses the one it removed, and it repeats this with every point. With so few, the line clings to the ones it has and misses a lot on the one it has not seen. What makes the warning go away is adding more points: with five it usually disappears. Overfitting is covered in detail later, in Fitting a curve.

What just happened

You have just done all three things.

The data are the points. Each one is a pair of numbers: where it is horizontally (x) and vertically (y). They could be hours of study and an exam grade, square meters and the price of an apartment, or anything that is measured in two numbers.

The model is the line. A line is fixed by just two numbers: how much it tilts and at what height it crosses the vertical axis. The tool writes it at the top right; with the ten starting points it is y = 0.687·x + 1.658. Those two numbers (0.687 and 1.658) are the model: everything it has learned from the ten points fits in there.

Training is searching for those two numbers. Not just any line will do: you look for the one that makes the mean of the squared errors as small as possible, the MSE you see on screen. They are squared so that an error above and another below do not cancel each other out, and so that a large error weighs much more than a small one. That is why the method is called least squares, and it is not new: Adrien-Marie Legendre published it in 1805, and in 1809 Carl Friedrich Gauss claimed that he had been using it since 1795 (Least squares, on Wikipedia).

For a line, those two numbers can be calculated in one go with a formula, and that is what the tool does every time you move a point. Large models have so many numbers that no formula gets them all at once, and they are adjusted in small steps, correcting a little on each pass (that way of training is the one in How a machine learns). The underlying idea is the same: look for the numbers that make the error smallest.

Predicting is using the line with an x that was not in the data. Open the same tool with the prediction at x = 4: the green point on the line and the reading x = 4 → y = 4.407. There is nothing more behind it: a prediction is the height of the line at that point.

The name of all this, regression, also has a history. It comes from a study by Francis Galton in 1886 about heights. Galton compared each child’s height with the mean of their two parents’ heights, and saw that the children strayed from the population’s average height less than their parents did: if the mean of the two parents was, for example, 6 cm above the average, the children also tended to be above it, but only about 4 cm: closer to the average. The same happened below the average with short parents. He calculated that the children stayed at around two thirds of their parents’ distance from the mean: they “regressed” toward it (Regression toward the mean, on Wikipedia). The name stuck for the method even though it has nothing to do with going backward.

The classic mistake

You might think a model understands the data. The one in this article is a line: it does not know what the points are, only where they are. If the points were hours of study and grades, the line would keep rising without limit, and with 50 hours it would “predict” a grade of 36 out of 10. It is not a calculation error: the line does exactly what it was asked; what it does not know is when it has stopped making sense. The tool does point it out to you: ask for a prediction at x = 9.9, beyond the last point, and the warning “Outside the range of the data: this is extrapolating.” appears below it. That warning does not come from the line: whoever made the tool put it there. In large models the same thing happens, with many more numbers.

What changes in your work

When an AI tool gives you a figure or a recommendation, it is doing the same thing as the line: applying what it learned from examples. It does not know whether your case looks like those examples. If you ask about something very different from the usual (an atypical customer, a new product, an odd year), the answer comes out with the same confidence, even though it no longer means anything. Before trusting the answer, ask yourself whether your case resembles what it learned from.

Try it yourself

In Regression & MLE, click Reset to go back to the ten starting points. Raise the first point on the left a little and see how much the tilt of the line changes. Put it back with Reset and do the same with the fifth, which is toward the middle. Which one moves the line more? Why do you think a point at one end weighs more than one in the middle?

And for the next step in the series: open the same tool with degree 7. It is no longer a line: the curve twists to get closer to the points, the MSE drops (from 0.236 to 0.134) and at the edges it shoots off. Now ask for the same prediction at x = 9.9 with this curve: the line said 8.461; the curve says 14.286. Is it a better model? Keep the answer for later (it is the subject of Fitting a curve).

items.title: Nvidia Introduced Alibaba to Alice Huang for Workaround on U.S. Export Controls
items.summary: Nvidia’s sales team introduced Chinese tech giant Alibaba to Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese spy involved in smuggling Nvidia chips into China, months before U.S. export controls on advanced semiconductors came into effect in 2022, according to three people with direct knowledge of the matter. Nvidia ’s introductions, which happened on two occasions across several months in 2022, helped Huang and her company land Alibaba as a customer, two of the three people said. From there on, Huang, a newcomer to the chip renting business, was able to get bank loans that helped finance the purchase of Nvidia chips, the two people said.

items.title: WebAIAssist: One Assistant for the Agentic Web
items.summary: An universal extension for the agentic web and knowledge nodes. A free, open-source Chrome extension that puts an AI helper in your side panel, with a local AI model running in your browser, lets it use the tools any web page offers, and interact with websites by chat. Web pages are learning to talk to AI assistants. With WebMCP, a page can say: here is what you can do on me, and here is how to ask. Search this catalogue. Read this article. Check this order. Search for Flights. There is a catch. A page that offers tools needs an assistant that can use them, and you should be the one who chooses that assistant. WebAIAssist is built to be that assistant for any page. It is a chat interface in Chrome’s side panel. It runs a small AI model on your own computer (or remote models if you have accounts and API keys), lists the tools the open page offers, and asks you before it uses any of them. On a page with no tools, it can still read the page and answer your questions about it. It is free and open source (Apache-2.0). There is no account and no analytics. You can install it from the Chrome Web Store . WebMCP in one minute An AI assistant can use a website in two ways. It can look at the screen and click around like a person, which is slow and breaks whenever the layout changes. Or the page can hand it a list of tools. WebMCP is the second way. A page registers its tools, each with a name, a description, and the inputs it accepts. An assistant running in the visitor’s own browser can then call a tool directly instead of guessing where to click. It is still a draft. The W3C Web Machine Learning Community Group is incubating it, with editors from Google and Microsoft. It is not a W3C standard, and it may change. In Chrome, you turn it on with a switch, which I explain below. What WebAIAssist does It works on any site with WebMCP tools. It is not tied to my own projects. Open a page, allow the site, and the panel lists the page’s tools with their descriptions and shows which ones only read data. You approve every call. Before a tool runs, the panel shows the tool, the site, and the exact arguments, and waits for you to press Allow once . You can let read-only tools skip the prompt for one site in one session, but tools flagged for review always ask. The extension never clicks, navigates, or fills in forms by itself. The model runs on your computer. You can pick a small model that runs on your graphics card (Qwen3 0.6B, Qwen3.5 2B, Llama 3.2 3B, or Gemma 4 E2B), one that runs on your processor (Qwen3 0.6B, Qwen3 1.7B, or Qwen3.5 2B), or Chrome’s built-in Gemini Nano. With these, your questions and the page text are not sent to a model service. The model files are downloaded once (about 350 MB to 2.8 GB for the first one). Or bring your own model. Point the panel at a local server such as Ollama or LM Studio, or at a remote OpenAI-style service like OpenRouter. With a remote service, your questions, the tool list, the tool results, and the page text you read go to that host. The panel asks you once for each host before connecting. It helps on ordinary pages, too. On a page with no tools, Read this page gives the model the page text to answer from. A site that says no to AI input in its robots.txt is respected: the model gets no text from it. Zero access by default. The extension is granted no site access at install. You allow one site at a time. It shows what a site says to machines. The panel reads and displays files such as llms.txt, robots.txt, and security.txt. Try it in two minutes You need Chrome 126 or newer (processor models require Chrome 137 or newer), or another Chromium browser. Install WebAIAssist from the Chrome Web Store . Enable WebMCP. Open chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing, set WebMCP for testing to Enabled , and relaunch Chrome. Without this switch, pages cannot show their tools. Open the side panel and pick a model. The first one downloads once. Open a page that offers tools, for example any page on agenticsystemcore.com , and allow the site. Ask a question. When the model wants to call a tool, read the call and press Allow . A site built for it: AgenticSystemCore 1.1 An assistant is only as useful as the tools a page gives it. So, here is the other half of my work. AgenticSystemCore is an open specification with a reference engine. It turns a folder of Markdown notes into a website, a knowledge graph, and files that agents can read. I released version 1.1.0 on 13 November 2026. It is a first that can gather and publish formatted texts as knowledge in a standard way, and could be used in multiple scenarios and types of work (such as: distributed second brain, auto-wiki with ontologies, nodes of semantic web and agentic knowledge web, collaborative project board, knowledge website, agentic system architecture, and other usages between agents and humans). Every page of a site built with it registers the same ten tools for WebMCP. They read, search, and cite. A change comes back as text for a person to merge. On these sites, WebAIAssist also adds a graph explorer and a read-only SPARQL view for ontology queries between documents. These same ten tools are available outside the browser through an MCP server for desktop assistants. I tested that the two paths agree. Version 1.1 is a new version, meaning a folder that was valid under 1.0 stays valid. Besides the tools, it adds: Stated meaning for every link. For each kind of link, the specification now defines its inverse, whether it carries along a chain, and what kind of note it should point to. Vocabulary tools. Export the graph as SKOS, or import a thesaurus as draft notes. SHACL shapes and a Dublin Core profile are generated from the schemas. An optional domain layer. A site can add its own classes and relations with checks. A site that does not use it builds the same bytes as before. A composition brief. It explains why each note is in a composed set, what it links to, the order of dependencies, and the gaps. SPARQL in the browser. The /query/ page runs queries over the site's own graph file locally. No server is involved. Firmer citation. Each chunk can carry a digest, the discovery document commits to the whole chunk set, and a result from the read tool carries a citation record. Memory adapters. Export and import for Mem0, Letta, Zep, CSV, Basic Memory, and Claude Code’s memory files. Nothing touches the network. To build your own site, you need Node.js 22.13 or later and git. In a folder with a few Markdown notes: npx -y agentic-system-core init mkdir -p .well-known && printf 'Contact: https://example.org/contact\n' > .well-known/security.txt git init -q && git add -A && git commit -q -m 'my notes' npx -y agentic-system-core ci npx -y agentic-system-core build init adopts your notes. ci lints, builds twice, and compares the bytes for determinism. build writes the site, the graph, and the agent files to www/. Running npx -y agentic-system-core mcp . gives a desktop assistant the ten tools over the same folder. What I measured How well small models pick tools. Small models choose tools less reliably than large ones, so I tested them on my own laptop in November 2026. Chrome’s built-in model called a tool on 5 of 5 questions, on both a test site and the live site. It finished the full expected sequence on 4 of 5 on each. Qwen3 0.6B on the graphics card picked the right tool on 8 of 10 questions on the test site, and 2 of 10 on the live one. Llama 3.2 3B and Gemma 4 E2B each ran past five minutes on their first question. The numbers for every model are in the repository . My advice today: start with Chrome’s built-in model, or connect a larger or remote one. T he site’s status page gives the command that reproduces tests and modes, current standards and specs. (Some numbers: Specification: 385 rules, 374 of them active; Conformance: 399 test vectors (376 pass, 0 fail, 23 withdrawn and replaced); Determinism: two clean builds, plus builds across time zones and locales. 61 files compared, 0 differ; Security floor: 108 of 108 seeded faults handled, 14 of 14 clean controls left alone; Engine: 4,964 tests, 0 failures, 58 skipped. Notes: the security line does not prove safety, and it does not cover new kinds of injection. It shows that the faults I know about are caught. And the Python package is a separate checker that runs 7 of the 20 areas of test vectors; it does not yet check the rest, so I do not claim two full implementations). What is not done WebMCP is a draft. It needs a Chrome switch today, and the draft specification may change underneath the extension. WebAIAssist is version 0.1.0. Its answers can be wrong, and small models pick tools unreliably. Safety is still on you. The extension cannot verify what a page’s tools really do. It shows you each call before it runs, but whether to trust the site is still your decision. AgenticSystemCore is complex. It is more complicated than a plain folder of notes. I would like to hear where the friction points are. No outside other projects uses it yet. Contributions welcome, in the GitHub issues or as a formal proposal. Every change, mine included, goes through the same review. The roadmap lists what later versions may add. Links WebAIAssist: Chrome Web Store Extension page Source AgenticSystemCore: Site and status page Graph explorer Source , npm and PyPI Specification preprint Software 1.1.0 record My earlier article on the release candidate Andrei N. Besleaga is a software architect and independent researcher based in Romania. He maintains the open AgenticSystemCore specification, its reference engine and website, and WebAIAssist. Written with AI assistance to organize and refine the prose. Author directed the draft, reviewed and edited it, and takes responsibility for statements. items.summary_html:
An universal extension for the agentic web and knowledge nodes.

A free, open-source Chrome extension that puts an AI helper in your side panel, with a local AI model running in your browser, lets it use the tools any web page offers, and interact with websites by chat.

Web pages are learning to talk to AI assistants. With WebMCP, a page can say: here is what you can do on me, and here is how to ask. Search this catalogue. Read this article. Check this order. Search for Flights.

There is a catch. A page that offers tools needs an assistant that can use them, and you should be the one who chooses that assistant.

WebAIAssist is built to be that assistant for any page. It is a chat interface in Chrome’s side panel. It runs a small AI model on your own computer (or remote models if you have accounts and API keys), lists the tools the open page offers, and asks you before it uses any of them. On a page with no tools, it can still read the page and answer your questions about it.

It is free and open source (Apache-2.0). There is no account and no analytics. You can install it from the Chrome Web Store.

WebMCP in one minute

An AI assistant can use a website in two ways. It can look at the screen and click around like a person, which is slow and breaks whenever the layout changes. Or the page can hand it a list of tools.

WebMCP is the second way. A page registers its tools, each with a name, a description, and the inputs it accepts. An assistant running in the visitor’s own browser can then call a tool directly instead of guessing where to click.

It is still a draft. The W3C Web Machine Learning Community Group is incubating it, with editors from Google and Microsoft. It is not a W3C standard, and it may change. In Chrome, you turn it on with a switch, which I explain below.

What WebAIAssist does
  • It works on any site with WebMCP tools. It is not tied to my own projects. Open a page, allow the site, and the panel lists the page’s tools with their descriptions and shows which ones only read data.
  • You approve every call. Before a tool runs, the panel shows the tool, the site, and the exact arguments, and waits for you to press Allow once. You can let read-only tools skip the prompt for one site in one session, but tools flagged for review always ask. The extension never clicks, navigates, or fills in forms by itself.
  • The model runs on your computer. You can pick a small model that runs on your graphics card (Qwen3 0.6B, Qwen3.5 2B, Llama 3.2 3B, or Gemma 4 E2B), one that runs on your processor (Qwen3 0.6B, Qwen3 1.7B, or Qwen3.5 2B), or Chrome’s built-in Gemini Nano. With these, your questions and the page text are not sent to a model service. The model files are downloaded once (about 350 MB to 2.8 GB for the first one).
  • Or bring your own model. Point the panel at a local server such as Ollama or LM Studio, or at a remote OpenAI-style service like OpenRouter. With a remote service, your questions, the tool list, the tool results, and the page text you read go to that host. The panel asks you once for each host before connecting.
  • It helps on ordinary pages, too. On a page with no tools, Read this page gives the model the page text to answer from. A site that says no to AI input in its robots.txt is respected: the model gets no text from it.
  • Zero access by default. The extension is granted no site access at install. You allow one site at a time.
  • It shows what a site says to machines. The panel reads and displays files such as llms.txt, robots.txt, and security.txt.
Try it in two minutes

You need Chrome 126 or newer (processor models require Chrome 137 or newer), or another Chromium browser.

  1. Install WebAIAssist from the Chrome Web Store.
  2. Enable WebMCP. Open chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing, set WebMCP for testing to Enabled, and relaunch Chrome. Without this switch, pages cannot show their tools.
  3. Open the side panel and pick a model. The first one downloads once.
  4. Open a page that offers tools, for example any page on agenticsystemcore.com, and allow the site.
  5. Ask a question. When the model wants to call a tool, read the call and press Allow.
A site built for it: AgenticSystemCore 1.1

An assistant is only as useful as the tools a page gives it. So, here is the other half of my work.

AgenticSystemCore is an open specification with a reference engine. It turns a folder of Markdown notes into a website, a knowledge graph, and files that agents can read. I released version 1.1.0 on 13 November 2026.

It is a first that can gather and publish formatted texts as knowledge in a standard way, and could be used in multiple scenarios and types of work (such as: distributed second brain, auto-wiki with ontologies, nodes of semantic web and agentic knowledge web, collaborative project board, knowledge website, agentic system architecture, and other usages between agents and humans).

Every page of a site built with it registers the same ten tools for WebMCP. They read, search, and cite. A change comes back as text for a person to merge. On these sites, WebAIAssist also adds a graph explorer and a read-only SPARQL view for ontology queries between documents.

These same ten tools are available outside the browser through an MCP server for desktop assistants. I tested that the two paths agree.

Version 1.1 is a new version, meaning a folder that was valid under 1.0 stays valid. Besides the tools, it adds:

  • Stated meaning for every link. For each kind of link, the specification now defines its inverse, whether it carries along a chain, and what kind of note it should point to.
  • Vocabulary tools. Export the graph as SKOS, or import a thesaurus as draft notes. SHACL shapes and a Dublin Core profile are generated from the schemas.
  • An optional domain layer. A site can add its own classes and relations with checks. A site that does not use it builds the same bytes as before.
  • A composition brief. It explains why each note is in a composed set, what it links to, the order of dependencies, and the gaps.
  • SPARQL in the browser. The /query/ page runs queries over the site's own graph file locally. No server is involved.
  • Firmer citation. Each chunk can carry a digest, the discovery document commits to the whole chunk set, and a result from the read tool carries a citation record.
  • Memory adapters. Export and import for Mem0, Letta, Zep, CSV, Basic Memory, and Claude Code’s memory files. Nothing touches the network.

To build your own site, you need Node.js 22.13 or later and git. In a folder with a few Markdown notes:

npx -y agentic-system-core init
mkdir -p .well-known && printf 'Contact: https://example.org/contact\n' > .well-known/security.txt
git init -q && git add -A && git commit -q -m 'my notes'
npx -y agentic-system-core ci
npx -y agentic-system-core build
  • init adopts your notes.
  • ci lints, builds twice, and compares the bytes for determinism.
  • build writes the site, the graph, and the agent files to www/.
  • Running npx -y agentic-system-core mcp . gives a desktop assistant the ten tools over the same folder.
What I measured

How well small models pick tools. Small models choose tools less reliably than large ones, so I tested them on my own laptop in November 2026.

  • Chrome’s built-in model called a tool on 5 of 5 questions, on both a test site and the live site. It finished the full expected sequence on 4 of 5 on each.
  • Qwen3 0.6B on the graphics card picked the right tool on 8 of 10 questions on the test site, and 2 of 10 on the live one.
  • Llama 3.2 3B and Gemma 4 E2B each ran past five minutes on their first question.

The numbers for every model are in the repository. My advice today: start with Chrome’s built-in model, or connect a larger or remote one.

The site’s status page gives the command that reproduces tests and modes, current standards and specs.

(Some numbers: Specification: 385 rules, 374 of them active; Conformance: 399 test vectors (376 pass, 0 fail, 23 withdrawn and replaced); Determinism: two clean builds, plus builds across time zones and locales. 61 files compared, 0 differ; Security floor: 108 of 108 seeded faults handled, 14 of 14 clean controls left alone; Engine: 4,964 tests, 0 failures, 58 skipped. Notes: the security line does not prove safety, and it does not cover new kinds of injection. It shows that the faults I know about are caught. And the Python package is a separate checker that runs 7 of the 20 areas of test vectors; it does not yet check the rest, so I do not claim two full implementations).

What is not done
  • WebMCP is a draft. It needs a Chrome switch today, and the draft specification may change underneath the extension.
  • WebAIAssist is version 0.1.0. Its answers can be wrong, and small models pick tools unreliably.
  • Safety is still on you. The extension cannot verify what a page’s tools really do. It shows you each call before it runs, but whether to trust the site is still your decision.
  • AgenticSystemCore is complex. It is more complicated than a plain folder of notes. I would like to hear where the friction points are. No outside other projects uses it yet.

Contributions welcome, in the GitHub issues or as a formal proposal. Every change, mine included, goes through the same review. The roadmap lists what later versions may add.

items.title: Google’s Gemini Decisions API Compared With Microsoft Decision 1, Jev, and OpenAI
items.summary: What each API can read, what it costs, and how the four performed in the Artificial Analysis Decision Index. Illustration generated with AI. On November 11, Google released the Gemini Decisions API and the model behind it, Gemini Decision 1 . You give it evidence and a fixed question. It can estimate the probability that a condition is true, choose from options you supply, or score something against a rubric. An app can use those answers to route a request or flag it for review. Google’s launch announcement · Decisions API documentation The part that caught my attention was the input. Gemini can evaluate text, images, audio, video, and PDFs. You can ask up to 1,000 independent questions about the same input in one request, within the context limit. Google AI Studio offers a playground and a free tier for prototyping. The paid rate is $0.10 per million input tokens, with no output-token charge. Gemini Decision 1 model card · Gemini API pricing Decision API inputs and pricing Microsoft Decision 1 accepts text or JSON through Microsoft Foundry, with a listed rate of $0.042 per million input tokens. When I tried it for UI checks, I struggled with the cases where the evidence I needed was visual. For decisions based on structured state or text, Foundry still appeals to me because it also offers models from OpenAI and Anthropic. Microsoft Decision 1 docs · Microsoft pricing announcement · Foundry model catalog TypeSafe’s Jev also lists $0.042 per million input tokens. I couldn’t attach images in the setup I tried, and bringing in a separate provider for one model felt like a lot of work for a company. TypeSafe now offers experimental image input, and Jev 1.14 can return a bounding box around a target in an image. OpenRouter also offers Jev and Gemini Decision 1, which gives teams already using it another way to compare them. TypeSafe’s release · Jev pricing · Jev on OpenRouter · Gemini Decision 1 on OpenRouter OpenAI’s Decisions API is generally available with GPT-6 Luna. It accepts text, images, and JSON and supports up to 400 questions per request. An image can be shared across the request or attached to an individual question. The API also supports prompt caching, with a listed rate of $0.10 per million uncached input tokens before applicable adjustments. All four APIs list zero charges for output tokens. OpenAI Decisions API documentation Author-created chart. Direct media inputs listed in the provider documentation on November 17, 2026. Google · Microsoft · TypeSafe · OpenAI Artificial Analysis Decision Index results The Artificial Analysis Decision Index v2.1 combines six evaluations covering document decisions, tool selection, knowledge, reasoning, and consistency when questions are rephrased. It weighs how confidently models answer alongside whether they get the answer right. Its tasks use text, so these scores tell us about decisions on that test suite. Image, audio, and video capability still needs its own evaluation. Decision Index · Methodology Index score, time per task, and estimated cost per million tasks Gemini Decision 1 via Google AI Studio · 66 · 211 ms · $345 Microsoft Decision 1 via OpenRouter · 62 · 274 ms · $143 Jev 1.14 via TypeSafe · 66 · 92 ms · $156 GPT-6 Luna (Decisions) via OpenAI · 60 · 206 ms · $339 Artificial Analysis snapshot, November 17, 2026. Scores are rounded. Time combines each evaluation’s median using the index weights. Cost is estimated for the benchmark’s tasks at listed prices. The Microsoft timing is for OpenRouter. Gemini · Microsoft · Jev · OpenAI Author-created chart. Time per task and estimated cost per million tasks for the routes measured by Artificial Analysis. Lower is better on both measures. Decision Index v2.1 Jev and Gemini rounded to the same score. Jev took less than half the time per task and cost less than half as much on this suite. For my own work, Gemini is still the one I’d try next when the evidence is an image or a recording. I can experiment in AI Studio alongside the other Gemini models, which makes it easier for me to justify trying a decision model in the first place. items.title: If Your AI Agent Breaks the Law, It's Your Problem
items.summary: Who is responsible: In the UK, a company answers for what its AI agent does with customers "in the same way you are responsible for what an employee does," even if a supplier built the agent. - What it can cost: Under the regulator's direct powers, which cover "some consumer laws," the penalty "can be up to 10% of your business' global turnover or £300,000 (whichever is greater)." - The chatbot precedent: A 2024 Canadian small claims tribunal ordered an airline to pay after its website chatbot gave a customer wrong information about fares. It called the idea that the chatbot answered for itself "a remarkable submission." - What founders should do: Decide which actions need a person's approval, keep a record of what the agent did and who asked for it, and be ready to fix mistakes fast. items.title: Nvidia bought itself a little breathing room in the Jensen Huang comeback fight
items.summary: Jensen Huang speaking at the Fireworks AI conference in San Francisco. Alistair Barr/Business Insider Nvidia raised its forecast on Tuesday, sending the stock higher in after-hours trading. Potential CEO successor Ian Buck joined the earnings call but didn't say a word. Huang's powerful supporters aren't giving up on their push to bring him back. Nvidia 's board and interim CEO did just about enough on Tuesday to keep the growing army of Jensen Huang supporters at bay. At least for a few days. "A clean quarter and guide strengthen the board's hand but do not close the question," Dan Ives, a tech analyst at Yorkville Ives & Co., wrote in a note to investors after the AI chip giant reported results. I listened to Nvidia's earnings conference call, and I thought interim CEO Colette Kress and board chair Harvey Jones performed well under extraordinary circumstances. Jones came out swinging. He said the board had no intention of reinstating Huang and made it clear that questions about the ousted CEO were off-limits. Nvidia shares fell after those comments. Then Kress quickly delivered some welcome news. Nvidia raised its revenue growth forecast for fiscal 2028. She also pushed back against concerns that the company might have to cut prices to compete, and said profit margins would recover after dipping in the current quarter. The stock rebounded. By late Tuesday, shares were up almost 5% in after-hours trading. So far, so good. Jones also said Nvidia would consider internal and external candidates for its next CEO. That brings me to the most intriguing moment of the call. The curious case of Ian Buck Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at Nvidia. David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images As the question-and-answer session began, Nvidia announced that Ian Buck, VP and president of hyperscale and high-performance computing, would join Kress to answer analysts' questions. This was a big deal. Buck is a serious technologist who helped invent CUDA, the software that makes Nvidia's chips so useful for AI. He's also spent more than two decades at the company and has close relationships with its biggest customers. Business Insider has a great profile of Buck , who has emerged as a potential successor to Huang. "His hat is in the ring," Ives said when asked about Buck's appearance on the call. Now Nvidia appeared to have an almost perfect setup. The board had ruled out Huang's return, Kress had reassured Wall Street about the business, and a respected internal technical leader was being introduced to investors. Awesome. Except Buck proceeded to say absolutely nothing. Not a word. I kept waiting for an analyst to ask him a question. Nobody did. And Buck never volunteered anything. That was soooo weird. If you're being floated as a possible CEO of one of the world's most important companies, and you get a chance to address Wall Street during a leadership crisis, surely you say something? Maybe Nvidia wants the strong, silent type as its next CEO. (Huang, as we've learned recently, hasn't exactly been the silent type ). Joking aside, if I were a serious Nvidia investor, I would have wanted to hear from Buck. "It was odd, but then again this situation is all odd," Ives told me after the call. The Jensen comeback campaign Meanwhile, Huang still has powerful, wealthy supporters who aren't going away. And despite the stock gains late Tuesday, Nvidia shares are still below their pre-Huang level — not a great look for the board. "His return to Nvidia is in all of our best interest," Shopify CEO Tobi Lutke wrote on X after Tuesday's results. He added that there could never be a true replacement for a founder like Huang. Ives agrees. "The 15% special meeting threshold, activist pressure, and the Commerce Department's position on the export investigation remain the next steps in the saga," he wrote. Billionaire activist investor Bill Ackman has already explained how shareholders could pressure Nvidia's board to bring Huang back. Under Nvidia's bylaws, shareholders representing at least 15% of the company's voting power can demand a special shareholder meeting, provided they've held their shares for at least a year. They could then seek to replace directors with people who support Huang's reinstatement. A new board could then reappoint him CEO. That's a formidable challenge. Removing directors without cause requires support from two-thirds of Nvidia's outstanding voting shares, according to the company's bylaws . And 15% of Nvidia, at current valuations, represents more than $500 billion in stock. Huang owns roughly 3.5%, leaving supporters needing another 11.5 percentage points. Who has that much money? Only some of the world's largest investment funds and sovereign wealth funds. Oh, and Elon Musk. Sign up for the AI Insider newsletter here . Reach out to me via email at abarr@businessinsider.com Read the original article on Business Insider
items.summary_html:
Jensen Huang speaking at the Fireworks AI conference in San Francisco.

Alistair Barr/Business Insider

  • Nvidia raised its forecast on Tuesday, sending the stock higher in after-hours trading.
  • Potential CEO successor Ian Buck joined the earnings call but didn't say a word.
  • Huang's powerful supporters aren't giving up on their push to bring him back.

Nvidia's board and interim CEO did just about enough on Tuesday to keep the growing army of Jensen Huang supporters at bay. At least for a few days.

"A clean quarter and guide strengthen the board's hand but do not close the question," Dan Ives, a tech analyst at Yorkville Ives & Co., wrote in a note to investors after the AI chip giant reported results.

I listened to Nvidia's earnings conference call, and I thought interim CEO Colette Kress and board chair Harvey Jones performed well under extraordinary circumstances.

Jones came out swinging. He said the board had no intention of reinstating Huang and made it clear that questions about the ousted CEO were off-limits.

Nvidia shares fell after those comments.

Then Kress quickly delivered some welcome news. Nvidia raised its revenue growth forecast for fiscal 2028. She also pushed back against concerns that the company might have to cut prices to compete, and said profit margins would recover after dipping in the current quarter.

The stock rebounded. By late Tuesday, shares were up almost 5% in after-hours trading.

So far, so good.

Jones also said Nvidia would consider internal and external candidates for its next CEO.

That brings me to the most intriguing moment of the call.

The curious case of Ian BuckIan Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at Nvidia.

David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images

As the question-and-answer session began, Nvidia announced that Ian Buck, VP and president of hyperscale and high-performance computing, would join Kress to answer analysts' questions.

This was a big deal.

Buck is a serious technologist who helped invent CUDA, the software that makes Nvidia's chips so useful for AI. He's also spent more than two decades at the company and has close relationships with its biggest customers.

Business Insider has a great profile of Buck, who has emerged as a potential successor to Huang.

"His hat is in the ring," Ives said when asked about Buck's appearance on the call.

Now Nvidia appeared to have an almost perfect setup. The board had ruled out Huang's return, Kress had reassured Wall Street about the business, and a respected internal technical leader was being introduced to investors.

Awesome.

Except Buck proceeded to say absolutely nothing.

Not a word.

I kept waiting for an analyst to ask him a question. Nobody did. And Buck never volunteered anything.

That was soooo weird.

If you're being floated as a possible CEO of one of the world's most important companies, and you get a chance to address Wall Street during a leadership crisis, surely you say something?

Maybe Nvidia wants the strong, silent type as its next CEO. (Huang, as we've learned recently, hasn't exactly been the silent type).

Joking aside, if I were a serious Nvidia investor, I would have wanted to hear from Buck.

"It was odd, but then again this situation is all odd," Ives told me after the call.

The Jensen comeback campaign

Meanwhile, Huang still has powerful, wealthy supporters who aren't going away. And despite the stock gains late Tuesday, Nvidia shares are still below their pre-Huang level — not a great look for the board.

"His return to Nvidia is in all of our best interest," Shopify CEO Tobi Lutke wrote on X after Tuesday's results. He added that there could never be a true replacement for a founder like Huang.

Ives agrees. "The 15% special meeting threshold, activist pressure, and the Commerce Department's position on the export investigation remain the next steps in the saga," he wrote.

Billionaire activist investor Bill Ackman has already explained how shareholders could pressure Nvidia's board to bring Huang back.

Under Nvidia's bylaws, shareholders representing at least 15% of the company's voting power can demand a special shareholder meeting, provided they've held their shares for at least a year.

They could then seek to replace directors with people who support Huang's reinstatement. A new board could then reappoint him CEO.

That's a formidable challenge. Removing directors without cause requires support from two-thirds of Nvidia's outstanding voting shares, according to the company's bylaws.

And 15% of Nvidia, at current valuations, represents more than $500 billion in stock. Huang owns roughly 3.5%, leaving supporters needing another 11.5 percentage points.

Who has that much money?

Only some of the world's largest investment funds and sovereign wealth funds.

Oh, and Elon Musk.

items.title: Intel cuts more jobs as CEO Lip-Bu Tan's efficiency push continues
items.summary: Intel just did another round of layoffs. Vernon Yuen/Nexpher Images via Getty Images Intel has laid off workers again, adding to a series of cuts this year. The job cuts add to a lengthy restructuring at the US chipmaker. Ongoing Intel restructuring has been focused on cutting management layers and refocusing projects. After a series of layoffs over the last two years, Intel has let workers go again in another round of cuts. The cuts are the latest sign that CEO Lip-Bu Tan's effort to make the chipmaker leaner is continuing into the final months of the year. This week, employees shared on social media about being affected by layoffs in Intel's global IT workforce. "As part of our broader strategy to become a more focused and efficient company, we continually assess our workforce to ensure priorities and resources are appropriately aligned," an Intel spokesperson said in a statement to Business Insider. Intel did not disclose how many employees were affected or identify the teams involved. The job cuts add to a lengthy restructuring at the US chipmaker, which has reduced its workforce and trimmed projects as it tries to revive its business after years of manufacturing setbacks and market share losses in AI chips. Intel has done several small rounds of layoffs this year. Tan, who became Intel's CEO last year, has said his restructuring plan was designed to lower expenses, reduce management layers, and shift resources away from lower-priority initiatives. Intel employed 81,100 people at the end of September, down from 85,100 at the end of 2025, according to company filings. Its headcount has fallen sharply since 2024, when Intel announced plans to cut more than 15,000 jobs, or about 15% of its workforce, under then-CEO Pat Gelsinger . Named victims featured vendors including Zoom, Paychex, Equifax, and GitLab, and end-user enterprises including Starbucks, IKEA, Mattel, American Eagle, Air France, Mutual of Omaha, Heineken, Home Chef, Cinnabon, American Eagle, Levi, Costco and HSBC. Salesforce issued a statement confirming that it had also been impacted by the attack. “Salesforce is investigating unauthorized modifications to scripts provided by Optimizely and used on certain Salesforce websites,” it wrote in an email statement. “As a precaution, Salesforce is confirming that Optimizely scripts are disabled across preview and production instances.” The attacks were discovered by UK-based security researcher Scott Helme , the founder of Report URI, who said in an interview that his team had confirmed 178 victims, but that there could be more. “That’s the number that we directly observed and that all carried the same infection,” he said. Helme published a report about the attacks on Monday, in which he described an attack methodology where an Optimizely capability in its Web Experimentation product facilitating adding members to a site’s development team was leveraged to insert malware into the sites. “The malware was a multi-purpose kit. It swapped cryptocurrency wallet addresses for the attacker’s, skimmed payment cards, stole cookies and screenshots, and on iPhones and iPads it delivered the Coruna and DarkSword iOS exploit kits,” Helme wrote. “The important lesson here is that trusted JavaScript doesn’t always remain trustworthy. A website can be compromised through a third-party dependency without its own code or infrastructure ever being breached.” Optimizely customers load a JavaScript “snippet” from Optimizely’s CDN onto their sites which contains Optimizely code, the customer’s A/B tests, and an optional field called Project JavaScript containing custom code written by the customer. The report said that attackers inserted their own code into the customer’s Project JavaScript and left the rest of each snippet untouched. “The file was still served from cdn[.]Optimizely[.]com, with Optimizely’s certificate, from a host that every affected site already trusted,” it noted. The report described how the observed attack worked. “The script watches form submissions and every fetch/XHR POST for a card number, expiry date and CVV,” it said. “When it has all three, it sends them to https://1688360[.]cc/card[.]php with navigator.sendBeacon . Cards entered in hosted payment iframes [such as] Stripe, Adyen and similar were out of its reach. Cards typed into a site’s own form fields were not.” Analyst questions the claims of a fix Optimizely, which did not reply to an interview request, confirmed the attacks on its site. In an email shared with customers, Optimizely said that attackers “exploited a vulnerability in the Experimentation account signup flow. They used it to impersonate a user and add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects. We have blocked access to the vulnerable path and deployed a fix.” The email also said that the company had “ended active sessions and revoked tokens and reset access for affected user accounts” and that it also had “removed the injected code from affected projects” and “blocked any code from being delivered in Cloudflare.” The company used highly confident wording to describe its fix, saying that “the Optimizely Experimentation platform is fully secured” and that “modification of Javascript no longer possible.” Frank Dickson , principal analyst at Dickson Research, raised an eyebrow at those claims. To begin with, he noted a discrepancy in the timelines published by the vendor and the security researcher. “Optimizely puts the first malicious write at 07:51. Report URI saw the BBC’s Optimizely snippet loading attacker code at 04:21, three and a half hours earlier,” he said. “The forensics report should reconcile that gap. Customers need the real start time to scope their exposure.” As well, he pointed out, “Optimizely seems very comfortable stating absolutes early in a forensics investigation. Those are verdicts from a company whose forensics are still underway and whose timeline disagrees with outside research.” No responsibility for the attack claimed Helme speculated in an interview that the attackers were a small group of thieves, almost certainly coming from China, noting that he saw extensive Chinese writing in the code and that the attacks “tie back to infrastructure that has been used by other Chinese actors.” “They are either Chinese or they really want us to think that they are Chinese,” Helme said, adding that the nature of what was stolen makes it highly unlikely the attackers were state actors. State actors, he said, would likely have used the malware on major news sites to create and spread false stories. Asked if his team could verify Optimizely’s claim that it had fixed the hole, he said that he couldn’t yet. Some of the infected sites were cleaned up, but he has to wait to see if they get reinfected before concluding that the original hole had been closed. Recommendation to customers ‘concerning’ Dickson said that one line in Optimizely’s email to customers was especially concerning. “Optimizely’s documentation tells customers to allow ‘unsafe-eval ‘ in their policy. At HSBC, the policy blocked the main payload and the data theft, but a backup copy of the malicious code ran anyway through that setting. A vendor’s setup guide should not quietly loosen its customers’ defenses,” Dickson said. “Restrict script-src to the hosts a page actually needs. Lock down connect-src so stolen data has nowhere to go. Drop ‘ unsafe-eval ‘ wherever possible. Start in report-only mode so nothing breaks.” He added, “the Optimizely attack may be about as bad as a third-party script compromise gets. Optimizely owes its customers a clear explanation of how one flaw reached so many unrelated companies.”
items.summary_html:
Attackers apparently from China used an authentication security hole within the popular Optimizely AI platform for marketers to steal from at least 178 sites owned by some of the planet’s largest companies. 

Named victims featured vendors including Zoom, Paychex, Equifax, and GitLab, and end-user enterprises including Starbucks, IKEA, Mattel, American Eagle, Air France, Mutual of Omaha, Heineken, Home Chef, Cinnabon, American Eagle, Levi, Costco and HSBC.

Salesforce issued a statement confirming that it had also been impacted by the attack.

“Salesforce is investigating unauthorized modifications to scripts provided by Optimizely and used on certain Salesforce websites,” it wrote in an email statement. “As a precaution, Salesforce is confirming that Optimizely scripts are disabled across preview and production instances.”

The attacks were discovered by UK-based security researcher Scott Helme, the founder of Report URI, who said in an interview that his team had confirmed 178 victims, but that there could be more. “That’s the number that we directly observed and that all carried the same infection,” he said. 

Helme published a report about the attacks on Monday, in which he described an attack methodology where an Optimizely capability in its Web Experimentation product facilitating adding members to a site’s development team was leveraged to insert malware into the sites.

“The malware was a multi-purpose kit. It swapped cryptocurrency wallet addresses for the attacker’s, skimmed payment cards, stole cookies and screenshots, and on iPhones and iPads it delivered the Coruna and DarkSword iOS exploit kits,” Helme wrote. “The important lesson here is that trusted JavaScript doesn’t always remain trustworthy. A website can be compromised through a third-party dependency without its own code or infrastructure ever being breached.” 

Optimizely customers load a JavaScript “snippet” from Optimizely’s CDN onto their sites which contains Optimizely code, the customer’s A/B tests, and an optional field called Project JavaScript containing custom code written by the customer. The report said that attackers inserted their own code into the customer’s Project JavaScript and left the rest of each snippet untouched. “The file was still served from cdn[.]Optimizely[.]com, with Optimizely’s certificate, from a host that every affected site already trusted,” it noted.

The report described how the observed attack worked. “The script watches form submissions and every fetch/XHR POST for a card number, expiry date and CVV,” it said. “When it has all three, it sends them to https://1688360[.]cc/card[.]php with navigator.sendBeacon. Cards entered in hosted payment iframes [such as] Stripe, Adyen and similar were out of its reach. Cards typed into a site’s own form fields were not.”

Analyst questions the claims of a fix

Optimizely, which did not reply to an interview request, confirmed the attacks on its site. In an email shared with customers, Optimizely said that attackers “exploited a vulnerability in the Experimentation account signup flow. They used it to impersonate a user and add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects. We have blocked access to the vulnerable path and deployed a fix.”

The email also said that the company had “ended active sessions and revoked tokens and reset access for affected user accounts” and that it also had “removed the injected code from affected projects” and “blocked any code from being delivered in Cloudflare.”

The company used highly confident wording to describe its fix, saying that “the Optimizely Experimentation platform is fully secured” and that “modification of Javascript no longer possible.”  

Frank Dickson, principal analyst at Dickson Research, raised an eyebrow at those claims.

To begin with, he noted a discrepancy in the timelines published by the vendor and the security researcher. “Optimizely puts the first malicious write at 07:51. Report URI saw the BBC’s Optimizely snippet loading attacker code at 04:21, three and a half hours earlier,” he said. “The forensics report should reconcile that gap. Customers need the real start time to scope their exposure.”

As well, he pointed out, “Optimizely seems very comfortable stating absolutes early in a forensics investigation. Those are verdicts from a company whose forensics are still underway and whose timeline disagrees with outside research.”

No responsibility for the attack claimed

Helme speculated in an interview that the attackers were a small group of thieves, almost certainly coming from China, noting that he saw extensive Chinese writing in the code and that the attacks “tie back to infrastructure that has been used by other Chinese actors.”

“They are either Chinese or they really want us to think that they are Chinese,” Helme said, adding that the nature of what was stolen makes it highly unlikely the attackers were state actors. State actors, he said, would likely have used the malware on major news sites to create and spread false stories. 

Asked if his team could verify Optimizely’s claim that it had fixed the hole, he said that he couldn’t yet. Some of the infected sites were cleaned up, but he has to wait to see if they get reinfected before concluding that the original hole had been closed. 

Recommendation to customers ‘concerning’

Dickson said that one line in Optimizely’s email to customers was especially concerning.

“Optimizely’s documentation tells customers to allow ‘unsafe-eval‘ in their policy. At HSBC, the policy blocked the main payload and the data theft, but a backup copy of the malicious code ran anyway through that setting. A vendor’s setup guide should not quietly loosen its customers’ defenses,” Dickson said. “Restrict script-src to the hosts a page actually needs. Lock down connect-src so stolen data has nowhere to go. Drop ‘unsafe-eval‘ wherever possible. Start in report-only mode so nothing breaks.”

He added, “the Optimizely attack may be about as bad as a third-party script compromise gets. Optimizely owes its customers a clear explanation of how one flaw reached so many unrelated companies.”

items.title: DOJ says it hasn't yet found any evidence of Saudi espionage in case against OpenAI engineer
items.summary: Abdulrahman Alfozan and his lawyer David Rizk speak to Judge Peter Kang in a courtroom sketch from Friday, November 3, 2026. Vicki Ellen Behringer Abdulrahman Alfozan is making another attempt to get out of jail. The Saudi national and former OpenAI employee is facing a wiretap charge. A US prosecutor said they haven't yet found evidence to charge him with espionage. Federal prosecutors say they haven't found any evidence yet that the Saudi national accused of bugging OpenAI's San Francisco office committed espionage or stole trade secrets. Abdulrahman Alfozan, who was arrested in mid-October, appeared in court on Tuesday as his lawyer sought his release from jail . "Government counsel acknowledged that if there were supporting evidence, new charges would have been brought when Mr. Alfozan was indicted," David Rizk, his attorney, wrote in a filing ahead of the court appearance. "Instead, Mr. Alfozan was indicted solely on the Wiretap Act count that was the subject of the Complaint." During Tuesday's hearing in front of US District Judge Vince Chhabria, Rizk demanded that the prosecution turn over discovery documents more quickly, saying they had floated the idea that Alfozan was a "spy," yet provided nothing to substantiate it. He also said he plans to return to the magistrate judge who ordered that Alfozan remain detained. When asked by Business Insider how Alfozan is doing in custody, Rizk said, "He doesn't like it." Federal prosecutors in San Francisco arrested Alfozan in October, accusing him of planting a listening device in a conference room at OpenAI's office, where he worked as an engineer. The criminal complaint accused him of the interception of oral communications. Prosecutors brought a grand jury indictment against Alfozan later in October and didn't include more severe charges, such as espionage or theft of trade secrets. He pleaded not guilty in early November . The prosecution is still looking through evidence, including footage from OpenAI On Tuesday, Judge Chhabria expressed concern that the prosecution might have overpromised during the October hearing that resulted in Alfozan's continued detention. The prosecution had said at the time that more charges might be brought. Nick Parker, the assistant US attorney leading the prosecution, said his team is still going through the evidence gathered for the case. That includes 160 hours of audio recordings, which he said appear to be from meetings at OpenAI. They are looking through Alfozan's and his wife's computers, as well as video footage from OpenAI. A power outage at an FBI facility locked Alfozan's cellphone, Parker said, so investigators hadn't yet been able to create a full forensic image. Alfozan agreed to provide the password after the hearing. Parker said also said that the recording device alleged to have been placed by Alfozan was encrypted, so the prosecution cannot access its current contents. Parker said he wasn't yet aware of any evidence that Alfozan committed economic espionage, stole trade secrets, or acted as an unregistered foreign agent. If the threat of those charges can be fully removed, Rizk said, "this case is going to completely change." He said that the prosecution had been moving too slowly in delivering him the evidence that he and his client need to fight the case. An agreement on AI use Judge Chhabria said that the prosecution should move quickly to provide additional material, including the contents of the laptops, the footage from OpenAI, and any reports prepared by FBI agents working on the case. Parker said that since there's OpenAI data on Alfozan's devices, there's reason to worry about Rizk using a competitor's AI model to look through the discovery documents. "I'm a lot less concerned about that than you are," Chhabria said in a deadpan. "You need to figure out a way to satisfy yourself on this, and you need to do it quickly." He told Parker and Rizk to reach an agreement on the use of AI by midday Friday. They also scheduled another status conference for December 8, a final deadline to submit discovery for December 11, and trial to begin the week of January 19. Parker said he suspects Rizk will delay the trial after getting the evidence. A different federal judge had earlier ordered that Alfozan must remain in jail while awaiting trial, ruling there was a high risk he would flee if released because the Saudi government offered to pay his bond and because his wife and son had already flown to Saudi Arabia . Photos included in Alfozan's criminal complaint show images of a USB device plugged into the back of a conference room TV and wrapped in toilet paper. The complaint also included what prosecutors said was a photo of Alfozan checking on the device a week after another OpenAI employee found it hidden there. Have a tip? items.title: Nvidia’s Board Rebuffs Jensen
items.summary: Well, that was embarrassing. A few hours after Nvidia’s recently departed CEO Jensen Huang issued a plaintive statement saying he’d love his job back, company chair Harvey Jones sent back a message: no chance, buddy. In an unusual appearance on the company’s earnings call Tuesday afternoon, Jones stated unequivocally that the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” Jones also added something the board didn’t say when it announced Huang’s exit last Thursday: that the exit came “after disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards and cultural norms.” So now it’s clear: it was Huang’s affairs (with a subordinate and a business partner) that caused his exit, and not, for instance, concerns about Nvidia’s possible involvement in smuggling of its chips into China.

items.title: Jeff Bezos has tips for the Nvidia board in choosing a successor for Jensen Huang
items.summary: Amazon founder Jeff Bezos says Nvidia's board should look internally for Jensen Huang's successor. Kimberly White/Getty Images for Semafor Jeff Bezos advised Nvidia's board to look internally for Jensen Huang's successor. Bezos said outsiders have a "vanishingly small chance" of succeeding at complex companies. Bezos said that whether Huang returns as CEO, he "deserves admiration and respect no matter what." Jeff Bezos has some advice for Nvidia's board as it searches for a permanent successor to Jensen Huang : The Amazon founder told Semafor's Liz Hoffman during the Silicon Valley & The World conference that Nvidia would be wise to look inside the company. "If you don't bring Jensen back, I would not hire an outsider," Bezos said. "NVIDIA is too complicated. "I think outside CEOs in complex companies have a vanishingly small chance of succeeding," Bezos added. "And so I would always think that's a last resort." Bezos, who stepped down as Amazon's CEO in 2021 after nearly three decades leading the company, said Nvidia's situation was different from Amazon's carefully orchestrated leadership transition, adding that his departure was the result of a "multi-year planned transition." Bezos's advice comes as Nvidia faces the challenge of replacing a founder whose leadership helped turn it into a central player in the AI boom. Huang, who resigned last Thursday amid reports of extramarital affairs and questions about a possible foreign intelligence effort, broke his silence Tuesday, saying he would be "honored" to return if the board determined it was in Nvidia's best interest. The board has said it does not intend to reinstate him. Nvidia Executive Vice President and CFO Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO while the company searches for a permanent replacement. The board is also investigating whether Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort. Huang's potential return has drawn support from employees and industry figures. An online petition calling for his reinstatement has garnered more than 190,000 signatures. When asked whether Bezos thinks Huang should be brought back, he declined to weigh in, saying he didn't know enough about what had happened behind closed doors. "Jensen is a remarkable guy who founded and built a remarkable company with a lot of hard work and foresight," Bezos said, "And he deserves admiration and respect no matter what, and that will never go away." items.title: Jensen Huang’s Right-Hand Man Oversaw Chip Customers—Including Alice Huang
items.summary: For years, anytime a major Nvidia customer wanted to buy chips or otherwise needed attention, they could turn to the company’s longtime former sales chief Jay Puri. That included Alice Huang, the former mistress of Jensen Huang, the Nvidia co-founder and former CEO who was pressured to resign last week by the company’s board, according to a person with knowledge of Nvidia’s operations. Alice Huang worked with a Chinese firm that secretly imported at least $7.5 billion of banned Nvidia AI chips into China, circumventing U.S. export restrictions, The Information reported . And Puri had a personal connection to another key customer, Supermicro, a server maker whose then-senior executives were criminally indicted in March for allegedly diverting Nvidia chips to China.

That included Alice Huang, the former mistress of Jensen Huang, the Nvidia co-founder and former CEO who was pressured to resign last week by the company’s board, according to a person with knowledge of Nvidia’s operations.

Alice Huang worked with a Chinese firm that secretly imported at least $7.5 billion of banned Nvidia AI chips into China, circumventing U.S. export restrictions, The Information reported. And Puri had a personal connection to another key customer, Supermicro, a server maker whose then-senior executives were criminally indicted in March for allegedly diverting Nvidia chips to China.

items.title: Copilot is "the new OS for work," and now Office runs inside of it
items.summary: Opening the keynote at its Ignite event, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella outlined the company's vision for its new "frontier ecosystem," announcing Tuesday the general availability of Word, Excel, and PowerPoint inside Copilot, which he described as "the new OS for work." The announcement is a striking inversion of how we've traditionally used software. Rather than an app like Word being the attraction and Clippy the assistant to help you use it, Microsoft envisions the new Copilot integrations will see agents driving things, with the software packages riding shotgun. Applications will become plugin components of the agent's work, backed by an organizational knowledge layer that draws context from emails, meetings, calendars, chats, and files. Users will now be able to create documents, spreadsheets, and presentations directly in Copilot, with the resulting files remaining editable in their respective Office applications. items.title: Ofqual urges ‘life-altering’ penalties for students who use tech to cheat
items.summary: England’s exam regulator says those caught using AI or smart glasses face disqualification from GCSEs and A-levels Students in England could suffer “life-altering” penalties if they are caught relying on AI or smart glasses to cheat, England’s qualifications regulator has said. The head of Ofqual , Ian Bauckham, said students could be disqualified from GCSEs, A-levels and other qualifications if they tried to use AI in assessed coursework, and called for retailers to be barred from marketing wearable technology for exam cheating.
